cards.prompt: Lithium toxicity ladder: what does each level look like, and when do you hold?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium toxicity ladder: what does each level look like, and when do you hold?
cards.answerHtml:
• Under 1.5: fine hand tremor, thirst, polyuria, GI upset; expected, often improve over time
  • 1.5 to 2.0: coarse tremor, confusion, sedation; withhold and notify
  • 2.0 to 2.5: tinnitus, extreme dilute polyuria, ataxia, seizures; speed excretion
  • Over 2.5: rapid coma and death; hemodialysis can be warranted

cards.prompt: Blood alcohol: what level is legal intoxication, and what level can kill?
cards.promptHtml: Blood alcohol: what level is legal intoxication, and what level can kill?
cards.answerHtml:
Legally intoxicated: 0.08%

Death possible: above about 0.4%

Quirk: learn the percentages (book prints "80 g/dL" and "400 g/dL", a units misprint)

cards.prompt: Caffeine and cannabis: which numbers does ATI give?
cards.promptHtml: Caffeine and cannabis: which numbers does ATI give?
cards.answerHtml:
Caffeine intoxication: above 250 mg; a 2-oz energy drink has 215 to 240 mg

Caffeine withdrawal: begins within 24 hr of stopping

Cannabis: motor impairment lasts 8 to 12 hr

cards.prompt: Lithium: when does it work, and when is the blood level drawn?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium: when does it work, and when is the blood level drawn?
cards.answerHtml:
Effect: 5 to 7 days; maximum 2 to 3 weeks; 2 to 3 doses daily (short half-life)

Draw: morning, 10 to 12 hr after the last dose

Frequency: every 2 to 3 days until stable, then every 1 to 3 months; recheck after any dose change

cards.prompt: Lithium: which kidney and thyroid labs, and why does sodium matter?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium: which kidney and thyroid labs, and why does sodium matter?
cards.answerHtml:
Kidney: BUN, creatinine (renal toxicity); baseline and periodic

Thyroid: T3, T4, TSH (goiter, hypothyroidism); baseline, then annually

Sodium: low Na (diuretics, sweating, vomiting) = less lithium excreted = toxicity

cards.prompt: Valproic acid vs carbamazepine: which levels and labs?
cards.promptHtml: Valproic acid vs carbamazepine: which levels and labs?
cards.answerHtml:
Valproic acid: 50 to 120 mcg/mL; LFTs baseline, then at least every 2 months for 6 months; platelets; amylase (pancreatitis); avoid under age 2

Carbamazepine: 4 to 12 mcg/mL; CBC and platelets (blood dyscrasias); sodium (hypoosmolarity)

cards.prompt: Olanzapine or clozapine: which metabolic and cardiac labs?
cards.promptHtml: Olanzapine or clozapine: which metabolic and cardiac labs?
cards.answerHtml:
Glucose: fasting, baseline and periodic (olanzapine, clozapine = high risk)

Lipids + glucose: if weight gain more than 14 kg (31 lb) (ch 25 prints 14 kg / 30 lb)

Cardiac (all antipsychotics): baseline ECG and potassium (QT, dysrhythmias)

cards.prompt: Sertraline or venlafaxine in an older adult: which lab?
cards.promptHtml: Sertraline or venlafaxine in an older adult: which lab?
cards.answerHtml:
Sodium: baseline and periodic

Why: hyponatremia, especially with diuretics

cards.prompt: Vomiting vs laxative abuse: what happens to bicarbonate and electrolytes?
cards.promptHtml: Vomiting vs laxative abuse: what happens to bicarbonate and electrolytes?
cards.answerHtml:
Vomiting: bicarbonate up (metabolic alkalosis)

Laxatives: bicarbonate down (acidosis)

Both: low K, Na, Cl, Mg, phosphate; high BUN; low albumin; prolonged QT

Note: ATI gives no cutoff numbers

cards.prompt: Sertraline (Zoloft): how long until it works, and when do sexual and weight effects appear?
cards.promptHtml: Sertraline (Zoloft): how long until it works, and when do sexual and weight effects appear?
cards.answerHtml:
Adults: up to 4 weeks (initial 1 to 3 weeks; maximal up to 2 months)

Children: initial 1 to 3 weeks; maximum by 12 weeks

Sexual dysfunction, weight gain: after 5 to 6 weeks

cards.prompt: Phenelzine (Nardil) washouts: how long before switching or surgery?
cards.promptHtml: Phenelzine (Nardil) washouts: how long before switching or surgery?
cards.answerHtml:
Stop phenelzine 14 days before: an SSRI, SNRI or buspirone (bupropion: 2 weeks)

Fluoxetine to phenelzine: stop fluoxetine 5 weeks first (children: 2 to 5 weeks)

Surgery: not within 10 to 14 days before or after

Children: at least 14 days before an amphetamine or TCA

cards.prompt: Amitriptyline vs bupropion vs venlafaxine: how long until each works?
cards.promptHtml: Amitriptyline vs bupropion vs venlafaxine: how long until each works?
cards.answerHtml:
• Amitriptyline (TCA): 10 to 14 days or longer; max 4 to 8 weeks; acutely ill get no more than a 1-week supply
  • Bupropion: 1 to 3 weeks; full effect 2 to 3 months
  • Venlafaxine, duloxetine: up to 4 weeks

cards.prompt: EPS timeline: when do dystonia, pseudoparkinsonism, akathisia and TD appear?
cards.promptHtml: EPS timeline: when do dystonia, pseudoparkinsonism, akathisia and TD appear?
cards.answerHtml:
• Acute dystonia: 1 to 5 days; spasms subside in 5 to 15 min with treatment
  • Pseudoparkinsonism: 5 to 30 days; watch the first month
  • Akathisia: 5 to 60 days; watch the first 2 months
  • Tardive dyskinesia: months to years; evaluate after 12 months, then every 3 months

cards.prompt: Haloperidol (Haldol): when does it help, and when does orthostatic hypotension ease?
cards.promptHtml: Haloperidol (Haldol): when does it help, and when does orthostatic hypotension ease?
cards.answerHtml:
Improvement: 2 to 4 weeks; full effect possibly several months

Orthostatic hypotension: tolerance in 2 to 3 months

NMS: first week or any time after

cards.prompt: Long-acting injections: how often is each given?
cards.promptHtml: Long-acting injections: how often is each given?
cards.answerHtml:
• Haloperidol or fluphenazine decanoate: IM every 2 to 4 weeks
  • Risperidone: every 2 weeks
  • Paliperidone ER: every 28 days; 3-month form every 3 months
  • Aripiprazole LAI: monthly

Effect: 2 to 6 weeks after first injection

Olanzapine ER: observe at least 3 hr after injection

cards.prompt: Disulfiram (Antabuse) and acamprosate (Campral): timing and monitoring rules?
cards.promptHtml: Disulfiram (Antabuse) and acamprosate (Campral): timing and monitoring rules?
cards.answerHtml:
Disulfiram:

  • first dose at least 12 hr after the last drink
  • reaction possible for 2 weeks after stopping
  • monitor liver function
  • no alcohol in any form (mouthwash, cough syrup, sanitizer)

Acamprosate: three times a day; avoid with kidney impairment

cards.prompt: Lithium: how much fluid and sodium, and which pain reliever?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium: how much fluid and sodium, and which pain reliever?
cards.answerHtml:
Fluids: at least 1.5 to 3 L/day (ch 30 prints 2 to 3 L/day)

Sodium: keep intake adequate and steady

Pain: aspirin, not NSAIDs

Hold and call: vomiting, diarrhea, heavy sweating

cards.prompt: Dry mouth and constipation from chlorpromazine or amitriptyline: what does the nurse teach?
cards.promptHtml: Dry mouth and constipation from chlorpromazine or amitriptyline: what does the nurse teach?
cards.answerHtml:
Fluids: 2 to 3 L/day

Also: sugarless gum, sips of water, fiber, void before the dose

cards.prompt: Lurasidone (Latuda) and asenapine (Saphris): how are they taken?
cards.promptHtml: Lurasidone (Latuda) and asenapine (Saphris): how are they taken?
cards.answerHtml:
Lurasidone: with food, at least 350 kcal, for absorption

Asenapine: sublingual; no eating or drinking for 10 min after

cards.prompt: Methylphenidate (Ritalin): when are doses given, and how long is the patch worn?
cards.promptHtml: Methylphenidate (Ritalin): when are doses given, and how long is the patch worn?
cards.answerHtml:
Last dose: before 4 p.m.; tablets 30 to 45 min before meals

Patch: no longer than 9 hr; shake suspension 10 seconds

Full response: up to 6 weeks (also atomoxetine)

Toxicity: chlorpromazine for hallucinations, diazepam for seizures, fluids

cards.prompt: Light therapy for seasonal depression: what dose?
cards.promptHtml: Light therapy for seasonal depression: what dose?
cards.answerHtml: Dose: 10,000 lux, 30 min/day

cards.prompt: Major vs persistent depressive disorder: how many findings, for how long?
cards.promptHtml: Major vs persistent depressive disorder: how many findings, for how long?
cards.answerHtml:
MDD: at least 5 findings, at least 2 weeks; weight change more than 5% in 1 month; postpartum onset within 4 weeks

Persistent: 2 years adults, 1 year children; at least 3 findings

Epidemiology: depression twice as common in females; anxiety comorbid in about 70% of depression

cards.prompt: Depression treatment phases: how long is each?
cards.promptHtml: Depression treatment phases: how long is each?
cards.answerHtml:
• Acute: 6 to 12 weeks
  • Continuation: 4 to 9 months
  • Maintenance: a year or longer (text: years; key: 1 year or more)

Drug course: continue 6 months after manifestations resolve, may be 1 year or longer

cards.prompt: GAD vs panic attack: which numbers define them?
cards.promptHtml: GAD vs panic attack: which numbers define them?
cards.answerHtml:
GAD: worry at least 6 months (key: more than 6; 6 months either way)

Panic attack: about 10 min; 4 or more manifestations

cards.prompt: Substance use disorder: which time window, and which ages are highest risk?
cards.promptHtml: Substance use disorder: which time window, and which ages are highest risk?
cards.answerHtml:
Criteria window: impairment over 12 months

Peak use: ages 18 to 25

Antidepressant suicide risk: mainly under 25

cards.prompt: Anorexia vs bulimia and binge eating: which numbers define them?
cards.promptHtml: Anorexia vs bulimia and binge eating: which numbers define them?
cards.answerHtml:
Anorexia: weight less than 85% of expected

Bulimia / binge eating: binge (and compensate) once weekly for 3 months; binge usually under 2 hr

Bulimia BMI: 18.5 to 30

cards.prompt: Somatic symptom vs illness anxiety disorder: how long, and how often is follow-up?
cards.promptHtml: Somatic symptom vs illness anxiety disorder: how long, and how often is follow-up?
cards.answerHtml:
Duration: both longer than 6 months

Screen: PHQ-15 = 15 symptoms

Follow-up: every 4 to 6 weeks

Conversion disorder: remission about 95%; relapse 20% within 1 year

cards.prompt: Crisis vs delirium vs neurocognitive disorder: what are the time frames?
cards.promptHtml: Crisis vs delirium vs neurocognitive disorder: what are the time frames?
cards.answerHtml:
Crisis: usually lasts 4 to 6 weeks

Delirium: onset hours to days; reversible, so find the cause

NCD: months to years; irreversible

cards.prompt: Restraint started in an emergency: when is the written order due, and how often does the nurse document?
cards.promptHtml: Restraint started in an emergency: when is the written order due, and how often does the nurse document?
cards.answerHtml:
Written prescription: within 15 to 30 min

Document: every 15 to 30 min during seclusion or restraint

Last resort: after de-escalation, PRN meds, less stimulation, one-to-one

Show of force: 4 to 6 staff (ch 31)

cards.prompt: Suicide precautions: what is documented, and how often?
cards.promptHtml: Suicide precautions: what is documented, and how often?
cards.answerHtml:
Every 15 min: location, mood, statements, behavior

Priority finding: the plan: lethality, specificity, access to means

cards.prompt: Mental status exam and adolescent screen: which numbers?
cards.promptHtml: Mental status exam and adolescent screen: which numbers?
cards.answerHtml:
Calculation: count backward from 100 by 7s

HEADSSS: 7 domains

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: how many, in how many clusters, and what age rule for antisocial?
cards.promptHtml: Personality disorders: how many, in how many clusters, and what age rule for antisocial?
cards.answerHtml:
Total: 10 disorders in 3 clusters

  • A: 3
  • B: 4
  • C: 3

Antisocial: needs conduct disorder before age 15

cards.prompt: Children and adolescents: which ages and counts does ATI test?
cards.promptHtml: Children and adolescents: which ages and counts does ATI test?
cards.answerHtml:
• Suicide: leading cause of death ages 10 to 24
  • DMDD: outbursts 3 or more per week in 2 or more settings; onset 6 to 18
  • ADHD: before 12
  • Conduct disorder, childhood-onset: before 10

cards.prompt: Family violence: which ages raise suspicion, and how many phases and steps?
cards.promptHtml: Family violence: which ages raise suspicion, and how many phases and steps?
cards.answerHtml:
Child abuse risk: under 4 years; any bruise before 6 months is suspicious

Cycle of violence: 3 phases

CISD: 7 steps (tertiary)

Nursing: report suspected abuse (all states); interview in private

cards.prompt: ECT, TMS and VNS: which schedule numbers?
cards.promptHtml: ECT, TMS and VNS: which schedule numbers?
cards.answerHtml:
ECT: 2 to 3 times a week, 6 to 12 treatments; atropine or glycopyrrolate IM 30 min before; 100% oxygen until breathing returns; alert about 15 min after

TMS: 3 to 5 days a week for 4 to 6 weeks, 30 to 40 min

VNS: pulse every 5 min for 30 seconds

cards.prompt: Grief models: how many stages each, and when is resolution expected?
cards.promptHtml: Grief models: how many stages each, and when is resolution expected?
cards.answerHtml:
• Kubler-Ross: 5 stages
  • Bowlby: 4 stages (seen from 6 months)
  • Engel: 5 stages; resolution about 12 months

Normal grief: some acceptance by 6 months

Depression stage: text and key word it differently; same stage

cards.prompt: Opioid overdose with respiratory depression: what is given, and what comes first?
cards.promptHtml: Opioid overdose with respiratory depression: what is given, and what comes first?
cards.answerHtml:
First: airway and breathing

Antidote: naloxone IM, SQ, IV or inhaled

cards.prompt: Lithium toxicity: how is excretion sped up?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium toxicity: how is excretion sped up?
cards.answerHtml:
Withhold: at 1.5 mEq/L or higher and notify

Remove: emetic (alert client) or gastric lavage

Speed excretion: urea, mannitol or aminophylline

Severe (over 2.5): hemodialysis

cards.prompt: Alcohol withdrawal: when does it start, and what is given?
cards.promptHtml: Alcohol withdrawal: when does it start, and what is given?
cards.answerHtml:
Timing: starts 4 to 12 hr after the last drink; lasts 5 to 7 days; delirium 2 to 3 days after (emergency)

First line: chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, lorazepam, oxazepam

Adjuncts: carbamazepine, clonidine, beta blockers (hold if HR below 50/min)

Nursing: seizure precautions

cards.prompt: Lithium 1.2 mEq/L in acute mania: give or hold?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium 1.2 mEq/L in acute mania: give or hold?
cards.answerHtml:
Exam-safe: give the dose; 1.2 is expected in acute mania and within maintenance 0.6 to 1.2

(text: acute range 1 to 1.5; answer key: 0.8 to 1.4)

cards.prompt: Involuntary emergency admission: who certifies, and when are the hearings?
cards.promptHtml: Involuntary emergency admission: who certifies, and when are the hearings?
cards.answerHtml:
Exam-safe: hearing within 72 hr, then another in 7 to 21 hr, as printed

(days would make sense; ATI prints hr)

Certify: usually 2 physicians

cards.prompt: Severe anxiety: can the client function and learn?
cards.promptHtml: Severe anxiety: can the client function and learn?
cards.answerHtml:
Exam-safe: no; cannot learn, problem-solve or take direction; functioning impaired

(ATI p.29 prints "functioning is effective", likely a misprint)

Nursing: short, simple, firm statements; stay; lower stimulation

cards.prompt: HIPAA and ADA: which years does ATI use?
cards.promptHtml: HIPAA and ADA: which years does ATI use?
cards.answerHtml:
Exam-safe: ADA defined mental illness as a disability in 1999

(the ADA itself dates from 1990)

HIPAA Privacy Rule: 2003

cards.prompt: Prazosin (Minipress) in PTSD: what is it for?
cards.promptHtml: Prazosin (Minipress) in PTSD: what is it for?
cards.answerHtml:
Exam-safe: know the use: reduces nightmares, hypervigilance and insomnia in PTSD

(ch 12: centrally acting alpha agonist; ch 21: listed as both central and peripheral alpha blocker)

cards.prompt: "I'm scared that you're going to leave me": borderline or avoidant on the ATI item?
cards.promptHtml: "I'm scared that you're going to leave me": borderline or avoidant on the ATI item?
cards.answerHtml:
Exam-safe: on that key item, pick avoidant

(text: abandonment fear = borderline; rejection fear = avoidant; use that elsewhere)

cards.prompt: Somatic disorders: which risk factors does the key mark correct?
cards.promptHtml: Somatic disorders: which risk factors does the key mark correct?
cards.answerHtml:
Exam-safe: anxiety disorder and childhood trauma

(the key calls age 16 to 25 a risk factor but does not mark it correct)

cards.prompt: Buspirone (BuSpar): how long until full effect?
cards.promptHtml: Buspirone (BuSpar): how long until full effect?
cards.answerHtml:
Exam-safe: about 1 week to start; several weeks for full effect

(ATI prints 2 to 6 weeks, up to 4 weeks, and 3 to 6 weeks)

Teach: take on a schedule, not PRN; not within 14 days of an MAOI

cards.prompt: Priority action in the initial interview
cards.promptHtml: Priority action in the initial interview
cards.answerHtml:
Priority: data collection, especially the client's own perception of their mental health

Comes after:

  • coordinating social services and family
  • teaching about the disorder

Data collection: ongoing at every encounter

cards.prompt: Levels of consciousness
cards.promptHtml: Levels of consciousness
cards.answerHtml:
Alert: opens eyes, responds fully to normal voice

Lethargic: responds but drowsy, falls asleep readily

Stuporous: needs vigorous or painful stimuli for a brief response

Comatose: no response to painful stimuli

Posturing: decorticate = flexion and internal rotation; decerebrate = neck and elbow extension, wrist and finger flexion

cards.prompt: Mental status exam: cognition checks
cards.promptHtml: Mental status exam: cognition checks
cards.answerHtml:
Orientation: time, person, place

Memory:

  • immediate: repeat numbers or objects
  • recent: same-day events
  • remote: verifiable past fact

Calculation: count back from 100 by 7s

Abstract thinking: interpret a cliché

Judgment: hypothetical ("fire in your room?"); expect a logical answer

cards.prompt: Mood vs affect
cards.promptHtml: Mood vs affect
cards.answerHtml:
Mood: the emotion the client reports feeling

Affect: the objective expression of mood (flat, blunted, etc.)

Also on the MSE: appearance, behavior, speech, cognition, judgment, level of consciousness

cards.prompt: Screening tools: MMSE, GDS, MAST-G, HEADSSS
cards.promptHtml: Screening tools: MMSE, GDS, MAST-G, HEADSSS
cards.answerHtml:
MMSE: cognition (orientation, attention/calculation, registration/recall, language)

Geriatric Depression Scale (short form): severity of depression in older adults

Michigan Alcoholism Screening Test: Geriatric: older adults

HEADSSS: children and adolescents

Pain: VAS, Wong-Baker FACES, FPS-R, McGill, PAINAD (advanced dementia)

cards.prompt: HEADSSS (adolescent assessment)
cards.promptHtml: HEADSSS (adolescent assessment)
cards.answerHtml:
Home environment

Education/employment

Activities

Drugs and substances

Sexuality

Suicide/depression

Safety (abuse at home, neighborhood violence)

Note: the client is the main source; caregivers add information

cards.prompt: Therapeutic strategy categories: which is it?
cards.promptHtml: Therapeutic strategy categories: which is it?
cards.answerHtml:
• Counseling: communication skills, problem solving, crisis intervention, stress management
  • Milieu: orient to setting, rules and boundaries, safe environment, activities
  • Self-care promotion: allow time to finish tasks, incentives
  • Psychobiological: give meds, teach, monitor effects
  • Cognitive/behavioral: modeling, operant conditioning, systematic desensitization
  • Health teaching, health promotion, case management

cards.prompt: Interview technique and older-adult questions
cards.promptHtml: Interview technique and older-adult questions
cards.answerHtml:
Technique:

  • private, quiet, well-lit space
  • ask preferred name
  • sit or stand at the client's level
  • summarize and ask for feedback at the end

Ask older adults about: sleep, incontinence, falls, dizziness, depression, loss of energy; add function, finances, home hazards

cards.prompt: Types of admission
cards.promptHtml: Types of admission
cards.answerHtml:
Informal: least restrictive; may leave anytime, even against advice

Voluntary: client chooses; competent, may refuse meds and treatment

Temporary emergency: unable to decide, current danger; hearing within 72 hr

Involuntary: indefinite; harm to self or others or unable to self-care; usually 2 physicians certify; client may request legal review any time

cards.prompt: Temporary emergency admission: hearing timeline
cards.promptHtml: Temporary emergency admission: hearing timeline
cards.answerHtml:
Hearing: court hearing within 72 hr

Second hearing: ATI prints "7 to 21 hr" (likely a typo for days (verify)); learn as printed for ATI

Qualifies: a current danger to self or others

Does not qualify alone: delusions, pacing, suicide attempt a year ago
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Five bioethical principles
cards.promptHtml: Five bioethical principles
cards.answerHtml:
Beneficence: doing good

Autonomy: client's right to decide, accepting consequences

Justice: fair, equal treatment

Fidelity: loyalty and faithfulness to the client and duty

Veracity: honesty (e.g., truthfully telling a client what staff discussed)

cards.prompt: Confidentiality and its exceptions
cards.promptHtml: Confidentiality and its exceptions
cards.answerHtml:
Law: HIPAA Privacy Rule of 2003; state laws vary

Share: only with those implementing the treatment plan, or with client consent

Exceptions:

  • duty to warn and protect third parties
  • child and vulnerable adult abuse

Privacy violation overheard: stop it first

Client says "don't tell" (hidden knife): tell them it must go to the team

cards.prompt: Seclusion and restraint: order and monitoring rules
cards.promptHtml: Seclusion and restraint: order and monitoring rules
cards.answerHtml:
Order limits: 18+ = 4 hr; 9 to 17 = 2 hr; 8 and under = 1 hr; rewrite every 24 hr

Emergency: may start without order; written order usually within 15 to 30 min

Monitor and document: every 15 to 30 min

  • food, fluids, toileting, vital signs, pain
  • behavior, meds, release time

Stop when: behavior safer and quieter; new order to restart

cards.prompt: Least restrictive first: escalating a response to aggression
cards.promptHtml: Least restrictive first: escalating a response to aggression
cards.answerHtml:
Order:

  • verbal: tell the client calmly to calm down or sit
  • low-stimulation environment, diversion or redirection
  • PRN medication
  • monitored seclusion
  • mechanical restraints last

Never for: staff convenience or punishment

cards.prompt: Intentional vs unintentional torts
cards.promptHtml: Intentional vs unintentional torts
cards.answerHtml:
Intentional:

  • false imprisonment: confinement not part of treatment (e.g., seclusion because short-staffed)
  • assault: threat
  • battery: harmful or offensive touching
  • invasion of privacy

Unintentional: negligence; malpractice = professional negligence

Negligence needs: duty, breach, proximate cause, cause in fact, damages

cards.prompt: Client rights and refusing treatment
cards.promptHtml: Client rights and refusing treatment
cards.answerHtml:
Rights: civil rights, informed consent, refusal, confidentiality, written care plan, outside contact, interpreter, dignity, freedom from harm, advance directive

Voluntary or involuntary: still competent; may refuse medication unless a court rules incompetent

Incompetent: court-appointed guardian consents

cards.prompt: Therapeutic communication: what it is
cards.promptHtml: Therapeutic communication: what it is
cards.answerHtml:
Is: client centered, purposeful, planned, goal directed (not social or reciprocal)

Essential components: time, attending behaviors, caring, honesty, trust, empathy, nonjudgmental attitude

Needs extra response time: major depressive disorder, schizophrenia

First step: establish a trusting relationship

cards.prompt: Clarifying techniques: restating vs reflecting vs paraphrasing vs exploring
cards.promptHtml: Clarifying techniques: restating vs reflecting vs paraphrasing vs exploring
cards.answerHtml:
Restating: the client's exact words ("You are having difficulty sleeping?")

Reflecting: directs focus back to the client's feelings

Paraphrasing: restates feelings and thoughts to confirm

Exploring: gathers more information on an important topic

cards.prompt: Question types
cards.promptHtml: Question types
cards.answerHtml:
Open-ended: spontaneous response ("Tell me about...")

Closed-ended: specific data; use sparingly, repeated use blocks communication

Projective: "what if" to explore feelings and solutions

Presupposition: hypothetical life without the disorder, to explore goals and motivation

cards.prompt: Barriers to therapeutic communication
cards.promptHtml: Barriers to therapeutic communication
cards.answerHtml:
• advice (interferes with the client's decisions)
  • false reassurance
  • minimizing feelings
  • "why" questions
  • personal opinions, value judgments
  • approval or disapproval
  • changing the topic
  • irrelevant personal questions
  • excessive questioning

cards.prompt: Techniques: presenting reality, focusing, offering self, giving general leads
cards.promptHtml: Techniques: presenting reality, focusing, offering self, giving general leads
cards.answerHtml:
Presenting reality: dispels delusions, hallucinations, faulty beliefs

Focusing: concentrate on one important point

Offering self: willingness to spend time

General leads: broad opening; client chooses where to start

Summarizing: reviews key points

Silence: time for reflection

cards.prompt: Levels of communication
cards.promptHtml: Levels of communication
cards.answerHtml:
Intrapersonal: self-talk; self-assess values before care

Interpersonal: one-on-one (psychosocial history)

Small group: team discussion, group therapy

Public: large groups (suicide prevention assembly)

Electronic: secure messaging, timely contact with providers

cards.prompt: Communicating with children, adolescents, older adults
cards.promptHtml: Communicating with children, adolescents, older adults
cards.answerHtml:
Children: simple language, eye level, play, watch your nonverbals

Adolescents: ask how they see the diagnosis; may refuse treatment to feel "normal"; check peer effects

Older adults: amplification if needed, face them, minimize distractions, allow plenty of time; ask caregivers about deficits

cards.prompt: Verbal and nonverbal communication elements
cards.promptHtml: Verbal and nonverbal communication elements
cards.answerHtml:
Verbal (6): vocabulary, denotative/connotative meaning, clarity/brevity, timing/relevance, pacing, intonation

Nonverbal (10): appearance, posture, gait, facial expression, eye contact, gestures, sounds, territoriality, personal space, silence

Red flag: verbal and nonverbal messages that do not match; culture changes interpretation

cards.prompt: Nurse's reply to a worried caregiver asking for reassurance
cards.promptHtml: Nurse's reply to a worried caregiver asking for reassurance
cards.answerHtml:
Best: "I understand you're concerned. Let's discuss what concerns you specifically." (reflects and accepts feelings)

Avoid:

  • "I'm sure everything will be okay" (false reassurance)
  • "Have you asked the doctor?" (avoids the concern)

cards.prompt: Levels of anxiety: mild to panic
cards.promptHtml: Levels of anxiety: mild to panic
cards.answerHtml:
Mild: sharpens perception, restless, irritable

Moderate: selective inattention, pacing, voice tremor, rising HR and RR; learning and problem solving still possible; benefits from direction

Severe: distorted perception, impending doom, hyperventilation, tachycardia; no learning; cannot take direction

Panic: loss of reality, delusions, hallucinations, dilated pupils, flight or immobility

cards.prompt: Nursing care: mild to moderate anxiety
cards.promptHtml: Nursing care: mild to moderate anxiety
cards.answerHtml:
• active listening, calm presence
  • open-ended questions, broad openings, exploring
  • evaluate past coping
  • explore alternatives
  • exercise to release tension (endorphins)

Avoid: false reassurance, ignoring the anxiety, closed-ended questions about feelings

cards.prompt: Nursing care: severe to panic anxiety
cards.promptHtml: Nursing care: severe to panic anxiety
cards.answerHtml:
Priority: safety; stay with the client and stay calm

  • quiet, low-stimulation space
  • short, firm, simple statements; slow, low-pitched voice
  • gross motor activity
  • direct attention to reality

Last: medication, seclusion or restraint, only after less restrictive measures fail

cards.prompt: Healthy defense mechanisms
cards.promptHtml: Healthy defense mechanisms
cards.answerHtml:
Always healthy:

  • altruism: reaching out to others (nurse who lost family in a fire volunteers as firefighter)
  • sublimation: unconscious substitution of acceptable outlet (gym after anger at boss)

All others: adaptive or maladaptive depending on frequency, intensity, duration

cards.prompt: Suppression vs repression
cards.promptHtml: Suppression vs repression
cards.answerHtml:
Suppression: conscious, voluntary pushing away ("I'll worry about bills next week")

Repression: unconscious; ideas forced out of awareness (keeps forgetting dentist appointments)

cards.prompt: Displacement vs projection vs reaction formation
cards.promptHtml: Displacement vs projection vs reaction formation
cards.answerHtml:
Displacement: shift feelings to a safer target (angry about job loss, destroys child's toy)

Projection: attributes own unacceptable feelings to someone else (accuses partner of an affair)

Reaction formation: shows the opposite of what is felt (praises disliked neighbor)

cards.prompt: Denial vs rationalization vs intellectualization
cards.promptHtml: Denial vs rationalization vs intellectualization
cards.answerHtml:
Denial: pretends the truth is not real (cough is "that cold going around" in a client with lung cancer)

Rationalization: acceptable-sounding excuse for unacceptable behavior

Intellectualization: separates emotion from facts (terminal client focuses on will and finances)

cards.prompt: Maladaptive-only defense mechanisms
cards.promptHtml: Maladaptive-only defense mechanisms
cards.answerHtml:
Conversion: unconscious physical symptoms without physical cause (deafness after divorce request)

Splitting: all good or all bad ("you're the only one who cares," then refuses to talk)

Projection: attributes own unacceptable thoughts to another (accuses partner of an affair)

Not on this list: undoing (can be adaptive; most common in children)

cards.prompt: Regression, compensation, identification, dissociation
cards.promptHtml: Regression, compensation, identification, dissociation
cards.answerHtml:
Regression: childlike behavior not fitting developmental level

Compensation: emphasizes strengths to offset weakness

Identification: takes on traits of another person or group

Dissociation: disconnection among identity, memory, perception (forgets identity after assault)

cards.prompt: Types of anxiety: normal, acute, chronic
cards.promptHtml: Types of anxiety: normal, acute, chronic
cards.answerHtml:
Normal: life force that motivates action

Acute: state triggered by imminent loss or threat to security

Chronic: sustained trait, often since childhood; fatigue, frequent headaches

Nursing: identify the level first; it drives the intervention

cards.prompt: Therapeutic vs social relationship
cards.promptHtml: Therapeutic vs social relationship
cards.answerHtml:
Therapeutic: client's needs, goal-directed, encourages behavior change, set termination date, clear boundaries

Social/intimate: mutual needs, emotional commitment, friendship

Empathy is therapeutic; sympathy (feeling as the client does) is not

cards.prompt: Transference vs countertransference
cards.promptHtml: Transference vs countertransference
cards.answerHtml:
Transference (client): sees nurse as a significant person; wants extra time, jealous of attention, compares to authority figure; likelier with authority figures

Countertransference (nurse): over-identifies, competes, argues, unexplained anger

Nursing: peer or clinical supervision

cards.prompt: Phases of the nurse-client relationship
cards.promptHtml: Phases of the nurse-client relationship
cards.answerHtml:
Orientation: introductions, contract (time, place, frequency, duration, termination date), confidentiality, trust, goals

Working: problem solving, test new behaviors, resistance, transference and countertransference, remind of termination date

Termination: feelings about loss, summarize achievements, plan to continue healthy behaviors, final

cards.prompt: Boundary issues: red flags
cards.promptHtml: Boundary issues: red flags
cards.answerHtml:
Blurred boundaries: relationship meets the nurse's needs or turns social

Example: client asks nurse to dinner = boundary issue, not transference

Nursing:

  • consistent level of involvement
  • reflect on boundaries often
  • seek peer or team supervision

cards.prompt: Physical safety in the milieu
cards.promptHtml: Physical safety in the milieu
cards.answerHtml:
• nurses' station placed for easy observation
  • no sharps or harmful objects
  • restricted and locked areas
  • monitor visitors
  • restrict alcohol, drugs, and sexual activity
  • deter elopement
  • rapid de-escalation by trained staff

Seclusion and restraint: only after less restrictive measures are exhausted

cards.prompt: Milieu therapy: goal and staff role
cards.promptHtml: Milieu therapy: goal and staff role
cards.answerHtml:
Goal: client learns to cope adaptively, interact better, strengthen relationships, and uses this in life

Staff:

  • fair treatment for all, allow choices
  • model good social behavior
  • maintain boundaries
  • promote independence, self-worth, hope
  • work as a team

cards.prompt: Community meeting
cards.promptHtml: Community meeting
cards.answerHtml:
Who: clients and nursing staff together; may be client-led

Topics: common unit objectives, common problems, discharge planning, upcoming activities, new clients

Not for: individual treatment plans or personal issues (use individual therapy)

Builds: communication, decision making, self-worth

cards.prompt: Therapeutic reply to a client grieving after a partner's death, at risk for suicide
cards.promptHtml: Therapeutic reply to a client grieving after a partner's death, at risk for suicide
cards.answerHtml:
Therapeutic: "Losing someone close to you must be very upsetting." (empathy)

Not therapeutic:

  • "You will feel much better with time. I promise." (false reassurance)
  • "Suicide is not the appropriate way to cope." (judgment)
  • "I know how difficult it is..." (shifts to nurse's experience)

cards.prompt: Roommate assignment on a 24-hr unit
cards.promptHtml: Roommate assignment on a 24-hr unit
cards.answerHtml:
Consider:

  • each roommate's personality
  • night disruption if a client cannot sleep
  • diagnoses: avoid pairing two clients with severe paranoia

Why: the milieu must stay safe and supportive for all clients

cards.prompt: Which setting? Partial hospitalization vs ACT vs community center vs home care
cards.promptHtml: Which setting? Partial hospitalization vs ACT vs community center vs home care
cards.answerHtml:
Partial hospitalization: short-term daytime care; home at night with a responsible person (some detox programs)

ACT: severe illness and nonadherent (e.g., forgets monthly injection); team goes to the client

Community mental health center: groups, med dispensing, counseling (no detox)

Home care: children, older adults, medical conditions

cards.prompt: Criteria for acute care admission
cards.promptHtml: Criteria for acute care admission
cards.answerHtml:
• clear danger to self or others
  • unable to meet basic needs
  • failed community-based treatment
  • dangerous decline in a client in long-term treatment
  • medical need plus mental illness

Goals: prevent harm, stabilize crisis, return to community care

Discharge planning: begins at admission

cards.prompt: Levels of prevention
cards.promptHtml: Levels of prevention
cards.answerHtml:
Primary: prevent problems (stress-reduction education)

Secondary: early detection (screening older adults for depression)

Tertiary: rehabilitation, prevent deterioration (support group after substance use program)

Trap: support group for those at risk of depression = primary

cards.prompt: Psychiatric home care: four criteria
cards.promptHtml: Psychiatric home care: four criteria
cards.answerHtml:
• homebound
  • psychiatric diagnosis
  • needs the skills of a mental health nurse
  • plan of care developed by the provider

Most used for: children, older adults, clients with medical conditions

cards.prompt: History of mental health care: dates
cards.promptHtml: History of mental health care: dates
cards.answerHtml:
Deinstitutionalization: Congress acts in 1946, 1955, 1963

Case management: about 1970

Managed care limits stays: about 1980

ADA (mental illness a disability, right to live in community): 1999 as ATI prints it

MBHOs: coordinate care, limit acute stays

cards.prompt: Prioritizing among clients in mental health settings
cards.promptHtml: Prioritizing among clients in mental health settings
cards.answerHtml:
See first: the client at greatest risk of self-harm (e.g., voice saying life is not worth living)

Later: burn, medication adverse effect request, situational anxiety

Inadequate discharge supervision: daily aide or weekly visits for a client needing supervision all day

cards.prompt: Acute care nursing roles
cards.promptHtml: Acute care nursing roles
cards.answerHtml:
• manage the unit and therapeutic milieu
  • safely give and monitor all medications
  • carry out treatment plans, assist with teaching
  • document the nursing process
  • manage crises

Team: nurses, psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, therapists, pharmacists

cards.prompt: RN vs advanced practice nurse; forensic and NAMI
cards.promptHtml: RN vs advanced practice nurse; forensic and NAMI
cards.answerHtml:
RN: manages care for a group of clients on a unit

APN: master's or doctorate; works independently, can prescribe, can manage a whole facility

Forensic nursing: evidence collection, victims and perpetrators of violence

NAMI: support and referral resource for clients and families

cards.prompt: Psychoanalysis vs psychotherapy vs behavioral therapy
cards.promptHtml: Psychoanalysis vs psychotherapy vs behavioral therapy
cards.answerHtml:
Psychoanalysis (Freud): unconscious, past, early childhood; months to years; seldom used alone today

Psychotherapy: more verbal, trusting relationship; 20 or more sessions

Psychodynamic: same tools, focus on present

Behavioral: present, learned behavior; no insight needed

cards.prompt: Free association and dream analysis
cards.promptHtml: Free association and dream analysis
cards.answerHtml:
Free association: spontaneous, uncensored verbalization of whatever comes to mind

Dream analysis: dreams play out unconscious urges and impulses

Used in: psychoanalysis

Teach: expect many sessions focused on past relationships

cards.prompt: Cognitive therapy and cognitive reframing
cards.promptHtml: Cognitive therapy and cognitive reframing
cards.answerHtml:
Premise: thoughts come before feelings and actions

Used for: depression, anxiety, eating disorders

Reframing: replace negative self-talk with supportive thoughts

Four techniques: priority restructuring, journal keeping, assertiveness training, monitoring thoughts

cards.prompt: Systematic desensitization
cards.promptHtml: Systematic desensitization
cards.answerHtml:
What: planned, graded exposure to a feared stimulus, imagined or real

Order: master relaxation first, then increasing exposure while using relaxation

Used for: phobias

Not: flooding (a great deal of the stimulus, therapist present)

cards.prompt: Flooding vs response prevention vs thought stopping
cards.promptHtml: Flooding vs response prevention vs thought stopping
cards.answerHtml:
Flooding: large exposure to the stimulus with a therapist present to extinguish anxiety

Response prevention: blocks a compulsive behavior until anxiety falls

Thought stopping: say "stop," substitute a positive thought; later say it silently

cards.prompt: Aversion therapy
cards.promptHtml: Aversion therapy
cards.answerHtml:
What: pairs a maladaptive behavior with an unpleasant stimulus (bitter taste, mild shock)

Used for: alcohol use disorder, violence, self-mutilation, thumb-sucking

Nursing: ongoing supervision and evaluation of those giving it

Example: alcohol causing nausea and vomiting

cards.prompt: Modeling vs operant conditioning
cards.promptHtml: Modeling vs operant conditioning
cards.answerHtml:
Modeling: client imitates a role model; improves interpersonal skills in the milieu

Operant conditioning: reward positive behavior (tokens exchanged for a walk with staff)

Add: positive feedback and encouragement

cards.prompt: Dialectical behavior therapy, validation therapy, and IPT
cards.promptHtml: Dialectical behavior therapy, validation therapy, and IPT
cards.answerHtml:
DBT: a cognitive-behavioral therapy for personality disorder with self-injury; gradual change plus acceptance and validation

Validation therapy: disoriented older adult; respect feelings in their reality

IPT: improves relationships, communication, role transitions, bereavement

cards.prompt: Matching the therapy to the client
cards.promptHtml: Matching the therapy to the client
cards.answerHtml:
Phobia: systematic desensitization

Panic attack: diaphragmatic breathing

Compulsion: response prevention

Intrusive negative thoughts: thought stopping

Depression with distorted thinking: cognitive reframing

Neurocognitive disorder: validation

Alcohol use disorder: aversion

cards.prompt: Group leadership styles
cards.promptHtml: Group leadership styles
cards.answerHtml:
Democratic: asks for suggestions, supports interaction and decisions

Laissez-faire: no attempt to control direction

Autocratic: leader fully controls direction and structure; no member decisions

cards.prompt: Phases of group development
cards.promptHtml: Phases of group development
cards.answerHtml:
Orientation: define purpose and goals; active leader; respect, trust, confidentiality; termination discussed

Working: problem solving and behavior change; power and control issues; informal roles; cohesion; leader's role fades

Termination: leader summarizes; feedback elicited

cards.prompt: Group member roles
cards.promptHtml: Group member roles
cards.answerHtml:
Task: carry out work (recorder; evaluates performance)

Maintenance: keep group going (harmonizer; praises input; follows direction)

Individual: own agenda, block teamwork (dominator, recognition seeker)

cards.prompt: Hidden agenda vs subgroup
cards.promptHtml: Hidden agenda vs subgroup
cards.answerHtml:
Hidden agenda: member or leader has goals differing from stated goals (members plan to embarrass a disliked member)

Subgroup: small set functioning separately (two members conspire to exclude the rest)

Both: disrupt group function

cards.prompt: Group types and settings
cards.promptHtml: Group types and settings
cards.answerHtml:
Open: members join as others leave; Closed: no new members

Homogeneous: shared characteristic (diagnosis); Heterogeneous: not chosen (all unit clients)

Acute unit: members vary daily, relief focus, more structure

Outpatient: consistent members, growth focus

cards.prompt: Areas of family functioning and dysfunctional boundaries
cards.promptHtml: Areas of family functioning and dysfunctional boundaries
cards.answerHtml:
Five areas: management, boundaries, communication, emotional support, socialization

Boundaries:

  • enmeshed: roles and feelings blend, unclear individuality
  • rigid: inflexible, isolated, little communication

Management: dysfunctional if chaotic or a child makes decisions

cards.prompt: Dysfunctional family communication patterns
cards.promptHtml: Dysfunctional family communication patterns
cards.answerHtml:
Blaming: shifts focus from own faults

Manipulating: dishonesty for own agenda

Placating: takes blame to keep peace at all costs

Distracting: irrelevant information during problem solving

Generalizing: "always" and "never"

cards.prompt: Scapegoating, triangulation, multigenerational issues
cards.promptHtml: Scapegoating, triangulation, multigenerational issues
cards.answerHtml:
Scapegoating: low-power member blamed for family problems

Triangulation: third person drawn into an unstable two-person relationship (parent allies with child)

Multigenerational: themes lasting at least three generations (substance use, dysfunctional grief, divorce)

cards.prompt: Family therapy: focus and nurse's role
cards.promptHtml: Family therapy: focus and nurse's role
cards.answerHtml:
Focus: the family as a system, not each person

Nurse:

  • focused interviews and family assessment tools
  • teach (medications, helping the ill member)
  • mobilize family resources
  • improve communication
  • strengthen coping

Discipline: consistent, timely, age appropriate, private, calm

cards.prompt: Acute stress vs prolonged stress: findings
cards.promptHtml: Acute stress vs prolonged stress: findings
cards.answerHtml:
Acute (fight or flight):

  • increased RR, HR, cardiac output, BP, metabolism and glucose use
  • depressed immune system, apprehension, decreased appetite

Prolonged (maladaptive):

  • chronic anxiety or panic, depression, chronic pain, sleep problems, weight change
  • higher risk of MI, stroke, hypertension, poor diabetes control, infection

cards.prompt: Stress screening tools
cards.promptHtml: Stress screening tools
cards.answerHtml:
• Holmes and Rahe Stress Scale (Life Change Units)
  • Perceived Stress Scale
  • Lazarus's Cognitive Appraisal

ATI gives no scoring cutoffs.

cards.prompt: Protective factors that increase resilience
cards.promptHtml: Protective factors that increase resilience
cards.answerHtml:
Resilience: ability to resist the effects of stress.

8 factors: physical health, strong sense of self, religious or spiritual beliefs, optimism, hobbies and outside interests, satisfying relationships, strong social support, humor.

cards.prompt: Cognitive reframing: thought restructuring vs priority restructuring
cards.promptHtml: Cognitive reframing: thought restructuring vs priority restructuring
cards.answerHtml:
Thought restructuring: replace irrational or negative thoughts with realistic, positive ones ("I'm a terrible father" becomes "I've made mistakes but I've improved").

Priority restructuring: prioritize differently to reduce the number of stressors (overworked client delegates tasks).

cards.prompt: Match the stress technique to the problem
cards.promptHtml: Match the stress technique to the problem
cards.answerHtml:
• Irrational thoughts: cognitive reframing, mindfulness
  • Too many demands: priority restructuring
  • Worry, need to identify stressors: journal writing
  • Rapid breathing, tension: breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery
  • Anxiety relief: exercise (endorphins)

cards.prompt: Biofeedback
cards.promptHtml: Biofeedback
cards.answerHtml:
What: trained professional uses a sensitive mechanical device to help the client gain voluntary control over autonomic functions.

Controls: heart rate and blood pressure.

Not: journaling (identify stressors), exercise (endorphins), or progressive muscle relaxation (tense then relax).

cards.prompt: Assertive statement: what to say
cards.promptHtml: Assertive statement: what to say
cards.answerHtml:
3 steps: describe the behavior, state your feeling, request a change.

Example: "When I have to pick up extra work, I feel very overwhelmed. I need to focus on my own responsibilities."

Nontherapeutic: disapproval ("You should..."), "why" questions, threats.

Key point: assertiveness changes the situation; mindfulness, exercise and support do not.

cards.prompt: Relaxation techniques for a client with acute psychosis
cards.promptHtml: Relaxation techniques for a client with acute psychosis
cards.answerHtml:
Nurse action: use nursing judgment about whether relaxation techniques are appropriate during acute manifestations of a psychotic disorder.

Not: teach every technique unchanged, or refuse all stress teaching.

cards.prompt: ECT: indications and risks
cards.promptHtml: ECT: indications and risks
cards.answerHtml:
Used for: major depression (med-resistant, suicidal or homicidal needing rapid response, psychotic features), schizophrenia with catatonia, schizoaffective disorder, acute mania (rapid cycling, unresponsive to lithium and antipsychotics).

No absolute contraindications. Higher risk: recent MI, hypertension, heart failure, dysrhythmias; stroke, brain tumor, subdural hematoma.

Not useful for: substance use, personality, dysphoric disorders.

cards.prompt: ECT: drugs given before and during the procedure
cards.promptHtml: ECT: drugs given before and during the procedure
cards.answerHtml:
• Atropine or glycopyrrolate: IM 30 min before; decrease secretions (aspiration) and prevent vagal bradycardia
  • Etomidate or propofol: IV bolus anesthetic
  • Succinylcholine: muscle relaxant after anesthetic; reduces injury; paralyzes respiratory muscles, so client needs breathing support
  • Stop benzodiazepines: they interfere with the seizure

cards.prompt: ECT: nursing care before, during and after
cards.promptHtml: ECT: nursing care before, during and after
cards.answerHtml:
Before: informed consent (next of kin or court order if involuntary), chest x-ray, labs, ECG; control hypertension and cardiac conditions; stop benzodiazepines.

During: IV line, EEG and ECG electrodes, 100% oxygen until spontaneous respirations return.

After: VS and mental status; client alert in about 15 min; expect brief hypertension; orient frequently.

cards.prompt: ECT: memory loss and what to teach
cards.promptHtml: ECT: memory loss and what to teach
cards.answerHtml:
Expect: confusion and disorientation for several hours; retrograde amnesia, short-term memory loss up to several weeks; most recover fully.

Nursing: frequent orientation, safe environment, help with hygiene.

Teach: ECT is not a cure; maintenance ECT weekly or monthly lowers relapse; anesthesia and muscle relaxant mean the old convulsion no longer occurs.

cards.prompt: ECT course and key numbers
cards.promptHtml: ECT course and key numbers
cards.answerHtml:
• Course: 2 to 3 times a week, 6 to 12 treatments for depression
  • Atropine or glycopyrrolate IM 30 min before
  • Alert about 15 min after
  • Rapid cycling: 4 or more manic episodes in 1 year
  • Theory: seizure boosts serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine

cards.prompt: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)
cards.promptHtml: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)
cards.answerHtml:
What: noninvasive MRI-strength magnetic pulses to the cerebral cortex; no seizure.

Use: major depression not responding to medication.

Course: outpatient, 30 to 40 min, 3 to 5 days a week for 4 to 6 weeks; client alert, no postanesthesia care.

Contraindicated: cochlear implants, brain stimulators, medication pumps.

Effects: tapping in head, scalp contraction, jaw tightening; seizure rare.

cards.prompt: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS)
cards.promptHtml: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS)
cards.answerHtml:
What: device implanted under the chest skin like a pacemaker; stimulates the vagus nerve.

Use: depression resistant to medication or ECT.

Pulses: usually every 5 min for 30 seconds; effect takes several weeks; client can turn it off with an external magnet.

Adverse: voice changes, hoarseness, throat pain, cough, dyspnea with exertion.

cards.prompt: ECT vs TMS vs VNS
cards.promptHtml: ECT vs TMS vs VNS
cards.answerHtml:
• ECT: induced seizure under anesthesia, muscle relaxant, 100% O2; memory loss and confusion
  • TMS: no seizure, awake, no anesthesia; scalp tapping, headache, seizure rare
  • VNS: implanted chest device, no seizure induced; voice changes, dyspnea

Trap: seizure and disorientation belong to ECT, not VNS.

cards.prompt: Panic disorder: the attack
cards.promptHtml: Panic disorder: the attack
cards.answerHtml:
Duration: about 10 min.

Needs 4 or more: palpitations, shortness of breath, choking or smothering, chest pain, nausea, depersonalization, fear of dying or going insane, chills or hot flashes.

Also: persistent worry about the next attack.

cards.prompt: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)
cards.promptHtml: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: uncontrollable, excessive worry most days for at least 6 months, with impairment.

Findings: restlessness, muscle tension, avoidance, extra time preparing, procrastination in decisions, poor sleep.

Rule out: hyperthyroidism, pulmonary embolism, medication effects, substances.

cards.prompt: Phobic and separation disorders
cards.promptHtml: Phobic and separation disorders
cards.answerHtml:
• Separation anxiety: fear when apart from attachment figure; headache, nausea, sleep problems
  • Specific phobia: irrational fear of an object or situation (acrophobia heights, zoophobia animals, monophobia being alone); may self-medicate with alcohol
  • Agoraphobia: fear of places where escape feels unsafe; avoidance
  • Social anxiety: fear of embarrassment in social or performance situations

cards.prompt: OCD and related disorders
cards.promptHtml: OCD and related disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Not true anxiety disorders.

  • OCD: obsessions relieved by compulsions (handwashing); done to reduce anxiety
  • Hoarding: cannot discard; unsafe home; more common in males
  • Body dysmorphic: preoccupied with a perceived flaw, mirror checking; greatest risk is self-harm or suicide

Tool: Yale-Brown (Y-BOCS).

cards.prompt: Anxiety: nursing priorities and communication
cards.promptHtml: Anxiety: nursing priorities and communication
cards.answerHtml:
• safety first; assess suicide risk
  • stay with the client; calm, quiet environment, few stimuli
  • open-ended: "Tell me about how you are feeling right now."
  • avoid advice, "why" questions, false reassurance
  • postpone teaching until anxiety subsides
  • ask about comorbid substance use

cards.prompt: Medications for anxiety disorders (ATI ch 11)
cards.promptHtml: Medications for anxiety disorders (ATI ch 11)
cards.answerHtml:
• Sertraline, paroxetine: first line for anxiety and OCD
  • Venlafaxine, duloxetine: also effective
  • Diazepam: short term only
  • Buspirone: can be taken long term
  • beta blockers, antihistamines also reduce anxiety

Teach: never adjust, stop or increase a dose without the provider.

cards.prompt: ASD vs PTSD vs adjustment disorder
cards.promptHtml: ASD vs PTSD vs adjustment disorder
cards.answerHtml:
• Acute stress disorder: at least 3 days, no more than 1 month after trauma
  • PTSD: longer than 1 month; can be delayed and last years
  • Adjustment disorder: mood or behavior change after a less severe stressor (job loss, breakup)

cards.prompt: PTSD: what the nurse sees
cards.promptHtml: PTSD: what the nurse sees
cards.answerHtml:
Intrusive: flashbacks, nightmares, distressing memories.

Avoidance: reminders; reluctant to talk about the event.

Mood: guilt, anger, detachment, cannot feel love or tenderness, negative beliefs.

Arousal: hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, insomnia, poor focus.

Screen for: suicidal thoughts or harming others.

cards.prompt: Dissociative disorders
cards.promptHtml: Dissociative disorders
cards.answerHtml:
• Depersonalization: observing own body or self from a distance
  • Derealization: outside world feels unreal or distorted in size
  • Dissociative amnesia: cannot recall personal information about trauma
  • Fugue: travels, cannot recall identity; weeks to months
  • DID: 2 or more distinct personalities

Rule out: TBI, epilepsy, substances (EEG, x-ray).

cards.prompt: ASD and PTSD: nursing care
cards.promptHtml: ASD and PTSD: nursing care
cards.answerHtml:
• therapeutic relationship; encourage sharing of feelings
  • safe, nonthreatening, routine environment
  • monitor for suicidal ideation; precautions
  • multiple anxiety-reducing strategies (music, imagery, massage, breathing)
  • child: involve caregivers, use play and art
  • crisis intervention right after the incident

cards.prompt: Dissociative disorders: nursing care and client teaching
cards.promptHtml: Dissociative disorders: nursing care and client teaching
cards.answerHtml:
Nursing:

  • help the client make decisions during dissociation, then encourage independence
  • routine decisions improve self-esteem
  • avoid giving too much information about past events

Teach: grounding (clap hands, stomp feet, touch ice, shower, touch objects), written journal, avoid caffeine and alcohol.

cards.prompt: EMDR and other trauma therapies
cards.promptHtml: EMDR and other trauma therapies
cards.answerHtml:
EMDR: rapid eye movements during desensitization.

Contraindicated: active suicidal ideation, psychosis, severe dissociative disorders, detached retina or glaucoma, unstable substance use.

Others: CBT (restructuring), prolonged exposure, psychodynamic, group, somatic therapy and hypnotherapy for dissociation, neurofeedback.

cards.prompt: Preventing PTSD after a mass casualty event
cards.promptHtml: Preventing PTSD after a mass casualty event
cards.answerHtml:
During: breaks, rest, water, food, emotional support, staff supporting each other.

After: debrief; encourage expression of feelings; use offered counseling.

Also: report suspected child abuse promptly; support high-risk groups (military, first responders).

Key point: talking helps; avoiding feelings does not.

cards.prompt: Medications for ASD and PTSD (ATI ch 12)
cards.promptHtml: Medications for ASD and PTSD (ATI ch 12)
cards.answerHtml:
• Paroxetine, sertraline, venlafaxine, mirtazapine, amitriptyline: relieve depression and anxiety
  • Prazosin: decreases hypervigilance and insomnia; ATI calls it a centrally acting alpha agonist, but it is an alpha-1 blocker (verify)
  • Propranolol: lowers vital signs, anxiety, panic, hypervigilance, insomnia

Adjustment and dissociative disorders: drugs only if depression or anxiety needs treating.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Major depressive disorder: criteria and findings
cards.promptHtml: Major depressive disorder: criteria and findings
cards.answerHtml:
Criteria: at least 5 findings, nearly every day, at least 2 weeks, most of the day (unipolar).

Findings: depressed mood, anhedonia, anergia, sleep change, poor concentration, indecisiveness, suicidal ideation, weight change over 5% in 1 month.

Look for: blunted affect, psychomotor retardation, poor hygiene, slowed speech, constipation, somatic complaints.

cards.prompt: Persistent depressive disorder, PMDD, SAD and postpartum
cards.promptHtml: Persistent depressive disorder, PMDD, SAD and postpartum
cards.answerHtml:
• Persistent depressive: milder, early onset, 2 years in adults (1 year in children), 3 or more findings
  • PMDD: luteal phase, 2 to 6%; exercise, diet, relaxation
  • SAD: winter; light box 10,000 lux, 30 min/day first line
  • Postpartum onset: within 4 weeks of birth; delusions endanger the newborn

cards.prompt: Depression: suicide risk and the priority action
cards.promptHtml: Depression: suicide risk and the priority action
cards.answerHtml:
Priority: safety first; assess risk, safety precautions, one-to-one observation as needed. It outranks ADLs, counseling and teaching.

Highest risk: acute phase.

Higher risk with: prior attempt, anxiety or panic, substance use, psychosis, poor self-esteem, no support, chronic illness.

cards.prompt: Depression: talking with a withdrawn client
cards.promptHtml: Depression: talking with a withdrawn client
cards.answerHtml:
• spend time with the client, even if silent
  • make observations ("I noticed you attended group today") rather than direct questions
  • simple, concrete sentences
  • allow extra time to respond

cards.prompt: Depression: phases of treatment
cards.promptHtml: Depression: phases of treatment
cards.answerHtml:
• Acute: 6 to 12 weeks; severe findings; reduce symptoms; highest suicide risk
  • Continuation: 4 to 9 months; prevent relapse
  • Maintenance: years; prevent future episodes

cards.prompt: Sertraline, fluoxetine, citalopram
cards.promptHtml: Sertraline, fluoxetine, citalopram
cards.answerHtml:
Class: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).

Use: leading treatment for depression.

Adverse: nausea, headache, insomnia, agitation, sexual dysfunction, weight gain.

Stop & report: serotonin syndrome; withhold the drug and notify the provider.

Teach: avoid St. John's wort; do not stop suddenly; effect takes weeks; report suicidal thoughts; avoid alcohol.

cards.prompt: St. John's wort
cards.promptHtml: St. John's wort
cards.answerHtml:
Class: herbal product, not FDA-regulated; used for mild depression.

Stop & report: potentially fatal serotonin syndrome if combined with SSRIs or other antidepressants.

Adverse: photosensitivity, rash, tachycardia, GI upset.

Teach: tell the provider; it can change levels of other drugs.

cards.prompt: Mania vs hypomania
cards.promptHtml: Mania vs hypomania
cards.answerHtml:
• Mania: elevated or irritable mood, at least 1 week; usually hospitalized
  • Hypomania: at least 4 days, 3 or more manic findings; milder, no hospitalization; can progress to mania

cards.prompt: Bipolar I vs II vs cyclothymic vs rapid cycling
cards.promptHtml: Bipolar I vs II vs cyclothymic vs rapid cycling
cards.answerHtml:
• Bipolar I: at least one manic episode with major depression
  • Bipolar II: hypomanic plus major depressive episodes
  • Cyclothymic: at least 2 years of hypomanic symptoms with minor depression
  • Rapid cycling: 4 or more episodes in 1 year; harder to treat

cards.prompt: Mania: what the nurse sees
cards.promptHtml: Mania: what the nurse sees
cards.answerHtml:
• labile mood, euphoria or irritability; intolerance of criticism
  • pressured talk, flight of ideas, grandiosity, distractibility
  • impulsive spending or giving away money, sexual indiscretions, poor judgment
  • manipulative, flashy dress, decreased sleep, neglects food and fluids
  • denial of illness

cards.prompt: Acute mania: milieu and safety
cards.promptHtml: Acute mania: milieu and safety
cards.answerHtml:
• Safety and physical health come first
  • monitor for suicidal thoughts and escalating behavior
  • decrease stimulation without isolating; seclusion only if needed
  • frequent rest, outlets for physical activity, short simple activities
  • protect from impulsive acts; remove dangerous items (belts, shoe strings, perfume)

cards.prompt: Mania: communication and limit setting
cards.promptHtml: Mania: communication and limit setting
cards.answerHtml:
• calm, matter-of-fact, concise
  • consistent limits; avoid power struggles
  • do not take comments personally; act on legitimate grievances

Gift offer: "I am here to provide care and cannot accept this from you."

Avoid: "why" questions and disapproval.

cards.prompt: Mania: exhaustion as a medical emergency
cards.promptHtml: Mania: exhaustion as a medical emergency
cards.answerHtml:
Why: a manic client may not stop moving, eat, drink or sleep.

Nursing:

  • prevent self-harm; decrease activity
  • ensure fluids and food (finger foods)
  • promote sleep; goal 6 to 8 hr nightly
  • assist with self-care

cards.prompt: Medications for bipolar disorder (ATI ch 14)
cards.promptHtml: Medications for bipolar disorder (ATI ch 14)
cards.answerHtml:
• Lithium carbonate: mood stabilizer (levels in ch 23)
  • Valproate, carbamazepine: acute mania
  • Lamotrigine: maintenance
  • Olanzapine, risperidone, chlorpromazine, loxapine: antipsychotics
  • Lurasidone, quetiapine: bipolar depression
  • Fluoxetine: major depressive episode

ECT: severe mania or suicidal, rapid cycling, when lithium fails.

cards.prompt: Bipolar: relapse triggers and client teaching
cards.promptHtml: Bipolar: relapse triggers and client teaching
cards.answerHtml:
Triggers: alcohol, cocaine, caffeine, sleep loss, stress.

Teach:

  • take medication every day, not only when relapsing
  • avoid caffeine
  • keep regular sleep, meal and activity routines
  • learn early relapse signs (sleep trouble, anhedonia)
  • psychotherapy, support groups, case management

cards.prompt: Schizophrenia: positive vs negative symptoms
cards.promptHtml: Schizophrenia: positive vs negative symptoms
cards.answerHtml:
• Positive (added): hallucinations, delusions, speech changes, bizarre behavior; easiest to identify and treat
  • Negative (absent): flat or blunted affect, alogia, anergia, anhedonia, avolition; harder to treat
  • Cognitive: poor decisions, memory, abstract thinking
  • Affective: hopelessness, suicidal ideation

cards.prompt: Psychotic disorders by duration
cards.promptHtml: Psychotic disorders by duration
cards.answerHtml:
• Brief psychotic: 1 day to 1 month
  • Schizophreniform: 1 to 6 months
  • Schizophrenia: at least 6 months
  • Delusional disorder: at least 1 month; function not markedly impaired
  • Schizoaffective: schizophrenia plus depressive or bipolar disorder

Onset: mid teens to mid 20s.

cards.prompt: Types of delusions
cards.promptHtml: Types of delusions
cards.answerHtml:
• Reference: trivial events have personal meaning
  • Persecution: being harmed (hunted by the FBI)
  • Grandeur: all-powerful or god-like
  • Somatic: body is changing (third arm)
  • Jealousy: unfounded belief of partner's affair
  • Being controlled: outside force
  • Thought broadcasting, insertion, withdrawal
  • Magical thinking: a hat makes them invisible

cards.prompt: Alterations in speech
cards.promptHtml: Alterations in speech
cards.answerHtml:
• Associative looseness: cannot stay on one thought; can reach flight of ideas
  • Neologism: made-up words
  • Echolalia: repeats others' words
  • Clang association: rhyming ("fox, box, lox")
  • Word salad: jumbled words
  • Circumstantiality: many unneeded details
  • Tangentiality: trivial topic instead of the main one

cards.prompt: Catatonia and altered behavior
cards.promptHtml: Catatonia and altered behavior
cards.answerHtml:
• Catatonia: marked decrease or increase in movement; catalepsy is rigid limbs staying where placed
  • Waxy flexibility: holds a position for long periods
  • Stupor: motionless, coma-like
  • Negativism: does the opposite of what is asked
  • Echopraxia: imitates others' movements
  • Automatic obedience, stereotyped behavior, agitation

cards.prompt: Command hallucinations: nursing action
cards.promptHtml: Command hallucinations: nursing action
cards.answerHtml:
Risk: harm to self or others.

First action: one-to-one observation for safety, then notify the provider.

Also: ask directly about the voices; do not argue or agree.

Watch: paranoid delusions can raise risk of violence.

cards.prompt: Talking with a client who has hallucinations or delusions
cards.promptHtml: Talking with a client who has hallucinations or delusions
cards.answerHtml:
• ask directly about hallucinations
  • do not argue with or agree with the belief
  • focus on feelings: "I don't hear anything, but you seem frightened."
  • steer to reality-based topics; avoid "why" questions
  • identify triggers (loud noises)
  • if client stares at the ceiling and talks: ask "Are you seeing something on the ceiling?"

cards.prompt: Haloperidol, chlorpromazine, fluphenazine, loxapine
cards.promptHtml: Haloperidol, chlorpromazine, fluphenazine, loxapine
cards.answerHtml:
Class: first-generation (conventional) antipsychotics.

Use: mainly positive symptoms.

Monitor: EPS: dystonia, akathisia, pseudoparkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia; use the AIMS for TD.

Teach: sugarless gum, fiber, fluids 2 to 3 L/day; rise slowly for postural hypotension.

cards.prompt: Clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, ziprasidone
cards.promptHtml: Clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, ziprasidone
cards.answerHtml:
Class: second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics; current drugs of choice.

Use: positive and negative symptoms.

Monitor: blood tests for agranulocytosis; weight.

Teach: low-calorie diet, exercise, weigh regularly; report agitation, dizziness, sedation or sleep problems.

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: overview and defense mechanisms
cards.promptHtml: Personality disorders: overview and defense mechanisms
cards.answerHtml:
What: pathological traits with impaired self and interpersonal function; client often sees nothing wrong.

Features: inflexibility, poor stress response, provokes conflict.

Clusters: 10 disorders in 3 clusters (A has 3, B has 4, C has 3).

Defenses: repression, suppression, regression, undoing, splitting.

cards.prompt: Cluster A: odd or eccentric
cards.promptHtml: Cluster A: odd or eccentric
cards.answerHtml:
• Paranoid: distrust, suspicious that others will harm
  • Schizoid: detached, indifferent to praise or criticism, isolates
  • Schizotypal: odd beliefs, eccentric, magical thinking; no clear delusions or hallucinations

Nursing (schizoid, schizotypal): respect need to isolate; do not push socialization.

cards.prompt: Cluster B: dramatic, emotional, erratic
cards.promptHtml: Cluster B: dramatic, emotional, erratic
cards.answerHtml:
• Antisocial: exploitation, no remorse, conduct disorder before age 15
  • Borderline: unstable mood, identity and relationships; splitting; fear of abandonment; self-injury
  • Histrionic: attention-seeking, flirtatious
  • Narcissistic: grandiose, needs admiration, lacks empathy

cards.prompt: Cluster C: anxious or fearful
cards.promptHtml: Cluster C: anxious or fearful
cards.answerHtml:
• Avoidant: avoids contact despite wanting closeness; extreme fear of rejection
  • Dependent: extreme dependency; urgently seeks a replacement when a relationship ends
  • Obsessive-compulsive: perfectionism, orderliness, control to the point of not finishing tasks

Nursing (dependent): assertiveness training, modeling, watch countertransference.

cards.prompt: Borderline personality disorder
cards.promptHtml: Borderline personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: unstable affect, identity and relationships; splitting (all good or all bad); manipulation, impulsivity, fear of abandonment.

Risk: self-injury and suicide.

Nursing: safety, consistent limit-setting, firm yet supportive care.

Therapy: DBT (acceptance and validation, gradual change).

cards.prompt: Antisocial personality disorder
cards.promptHtml: Antisocial personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: disregard for others, deceit, manipulation, no responsibility, charming, impulsive, conduct disorder before age 15.

Nursing: safety, firm consistent limits, do not be manipulated; watch for violence and substance use.

Example: "I'll go to group if you let me smoke."

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: nursing care priorities
cards.promptHtml: Personality disorders: nursing care priorities
cards.answerHtml:
• safety (self-injury, violence)
  • nurse self-assessment; these clients provoke strong feelings
  • firm yet supportive, consistent care
  • offer realistic choices; ask for input on schedule
  • limit-setting for borderline and antisocial
  • professional boundaries with histrionic clients

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: match the statement
cards.promptHtml: Personality disorders: match the statement
cards.answerHtml:
• "I need everyone to admire me": narcissistic
  • "I sometimes feel better if I cut myself": borderline
  • "I'll go to group if you let me smoke": antisocial
  • odd beliefs, magical thinking: schizotypal
  • perfectionism: obsessive-compulsive
  • social anxiety: avoidant

ATI trap: ATI's key marks "I'm scared you'll leave me" correct for avoidant, though ATI's text lists abandonment fear under borderline.

cards.prompt: Delirium vs major neurocognitive disorder (dementia)
cards.promptHtml: Delirium vs major neurocognitive disorder (dementia)
cards.answerHtml:
Delirium: rapid onset (hours–days), fluctuates (worse night/early morning), LOC altered, vital signs unstable, reversible; medical emergency, treat the cause

Major NCD: gradual (months–years), stable through the day, LOC unchanged, irreversible, progressive

Delirium types: hyperactive, hypoactive, mixed, unclassified

cards.prompt: NCD terms: confabulation, perseveration, aphasia, agnosia, apraxia, sundowning
cards.promptHtml: NCD terms: confabulation, perseveration, aphasia, agnosia, apraxia, sundowning
cards.answerHtml:
Confabulation: makes up stories to save self-esteem (not lying)

Perseveration: repeats phrases/behavior to avoid answering

Denial: refuses to believe memory loss

Aphasia: speech impairment

Agnosia: cannot recognize familiar objects

Apraxia: movement impairment

Sundowning: late-day agitation

cards.prompt: Diagnosing NCD and delirium: tests and tools
cards.promptHtml: Diagnosing NCD and delirium: tests and tools
cards.answerHtml:
NCD: no specific test; definitive diagnosis only at autopsy. Tests rule out other causes (B12/folate, thyroid, electrolytes, CT/PET, EEG).

Delirium tools: CAM, NEECHAM

Other tools: MMSE, FAST, Global Deterioration Scale, Functional Dementia Scale

Short Blessed Test: interview with a family member

cards.prompt: Safe environment for a client with delirium or dementia
cards.promptHtml: Safe environment for a client with delirium or dementia
cards.answerHtml:
Nursing:

  • room near nurses' station, low stimulation, well-lit
  • clocks, calendars, window, familiar objects
  • ID bracelet, bed alarm, lowered bed
  • cover or remove mirrors
  • allow safe pacing
  • restraints only as a last resort; careful with PRN drugs
  • eyeglasses, hearing aids, fluids, sleep

cards.prompt: Communicating with a client who has NCD or delirium
cards.promptHtml: Communicating with a client who has NCD or delirium
cards.answerHtml:
Do:

  • introduce self at every contact
  • short simple sentences, one idea at a time
  • calm tone, positive wording
  • reinforce reality; approach from the front

Don't:

  • argue with or question hallucinations
  • ask "why" or confront

Say: "I am your nurse. Let's walk to your room."

cards.prompt: Donepezil (Aricept), rivastigmine (Exelon), galantamine (Razadyne)
cards.promptHtml: Donepezil (Aricept), rivastigmine (Exelon), galantamine (Razadyne)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: cholinesterase inhibitor (more acetylcholine)

Use: slow decline in mild to moderate Alzheimer's

Stop & report: bradycardia, syncope; N/V/diarrhea (fluid loss)

Teach:

  • donepezil once daily at bedtime; galantamine and rivastigmine twice daily; rivastigmine patch once daily, oral with food
  • avoid NSAIDs (GI bleed) and cholinergic blockers (antihistamines, TCAs); caution in asthma/COPD

Taper: do not stop abruptly

cards.prompt: Memantine (Namenda)
cards.promptHtml: Memantine (Namenda)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: blocks calcium entry into nerve cells (slows cell death)

Use: moderate to severe Alzheimer's; can be combined with a cholinesterase inhibitor

Monitor: dizziness, headache, confusion, constipation

Teach: with or without food

cards.prompt: Home safety and caregiver teaching for dementia
cards.promptHtml: Home safety and caregiver teaching for dementia
cards.answerHtml:
Home:

  • remove scatter rugs; high door locks
  • good lighting, colored tape on steps, stair handrails
  • mattress on floor; cords secured; cleaning supplies locked; lower water heater

Caregiver: legal counsel (advance directive, POA), respite care, support groups

Late stage: choking risk, no finger foods

cards.prompt: Alcohol: intoxication vs withdrawal
cards.promptHtml: Alcohol: intoxication vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: slurred speech, nystagmus, poor judgment, decreased LOC, respiratory arrest. BAC 0.08% legal intoxication; death possible above 0.4%.

Withdrawal (CNS excitation): tremors, tachycardia, hypertension, increased temperature and RR, anxiety, transient hallucinations, tonic-clonic seizures

Priority: safety, seizure precautions

Chronic use: fatty liver/cirrhosis, gastritis, pancreatitis

cards.prompt: Alcohol withdrawal delirium
cards.promptHtml: Alcohol withdrawal delirium
cards.answerHtml:
Timing: 2 to 3 days after stopping alcohol

Looks like: severe disorientation, hallucinations, severe hypertension, dysrhythmias

Risk: medical emergency; can progress to death

Nursing: acute care, close observation, seizure precautions, low stimulation, give withdrawal drugs as prescribed

cards.prompt: Opioids: intoxication vs withdrawal, and the antidote
cards.promptHtml: Opioids: intoxication vs withdrawal, and the antidote
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: pupillary changes, slurred speech, decreased respirations and LOC (can be fatal)

Antidote: naloxone

Withdrawal: sweating, rhinorrhea, piloerection (gooseflesh), tremors, diarrhea, N/V, dilated pupils, bone/muscle pain

Key: very unpleasant but not life-threatening

cards.prompt: Diazepam and pentobarbital: intoxication vs withdrawal
cards.promptHtml: Diazepam and pentobarbital: intoxication vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: drowsiness, slurred speech, incoordination, nystagmus; respiratory depression and decreased LOC can be fatal

Antidote: flumazenil for benzodiazepines; none for barbiturates

Withdrawal: anxiety, hypertension, tremors, hallucinations, psychosis, seizures

Key: withdrawal can be life-threatening

cards.prompt: Cocaine and amphetamines: intoxication vs withdrawal
cards.promptHtml: Cocaine and amphetamines: intoxication vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Cocaine toxicity: tachycardia, hypertension, chest pain, hyperthermia, seizures, cardiovascular collapse

Amphetamines: increased HR/BP/temp, stroke, kidney failure, paranoia, psychosis, dental damage

Withdrawal ("crash"): depression, fatigue, craving, sleep changes; not life-threatening

Watch: suicidal ideation in cocaine withdrawal

cards.prompt: Cannabis, inhalants, hallucinogens
cards.promptHtml: Cannabis, inhalants, hallucinogens
cards.answerHtml:
Cannabis: increased appetite, dry mouth, tachycardia; paranoia at high doses; motor impairment 8 to 12 hr. Withdrawal: irritability, anxiety, insomnia, decreased appetite.

Inhalants: dizziness, nystagmus, hyporeflexia, respiratory depression; no withdrawal

Hallucinogens (LSD, PCP): panic, paranoia, dilated pupils; flashbacks can recur for years

cards.prompt: Caffeine and nicotine: intoxication and withdrawal
cards.promptHtml: Caffeine and nicotine: intoxication and withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Caffeine: intoxication above 250 mg (2-oz energy drink 215 to 240 mg): tachycardia, restlessness, diuresis, insomnia. Withdrawal within 24 hr: headache, irritability, drowsiness.

Nicotine: withdrawal is irritability, craving, anxiety, increased appetite, depressed mood; not life-threatening

cards.prompt: Nursing care for substance intoxication and withdrawal
cards.promptHtml: Nursing care for substance intoxication and withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Nursing:

  • safety first: falls, seizure precautions, close observation
  • restraints last resort
  • monitor VS and neuro status; low stimulation
  • watch for covert use during detox
  • stay nonjudgmental; self-assess

Teach: goal is abstinence; remove unused meds; enabling (calling in sick) is codependency; dual diagnosis treated together

cards.prompt: Medications and antidotes for substance use (ATI ch 18)
cards.promptHtml: Medications and antidotes for substance use (ATI ch 18)
cards.answerHtml:
