Alcohol withdrawal: diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, carbamazepine, clonidine, phenobarbital

Alcohol abstinence: disulfiram, naltrexone, acamprosate (no hidden alcohol with disulfiram)

Opioid: methadone, clonidine, buprenorphine, naltrexone

Nicotine: bupropion, nicotine replacement, varenicline

Antidotes: naloxone (opioids), flumazenil (benzodiazepines)

cards.prompt: Anorexia nervosa
cards.promptHtml: Anorexia nervosa
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: restricted intake, fear of weight gain, distorted body image, weight less than 85% of expected

Findings: lanugo, amenorrhea, low BP/pulse/temp, orthostatic hypotension, osteoporosis

Types: restricting; binge-eating/purging (more impulsive, more substance use)

Risk: suicide, high mortality

cards.prompt: Bulimia nervosa
cards.promptHtml: Bulimia nervosa
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: binge (usually under 2 hr, loss of control) then compensating, on average weekly for 3 months

Weight: normal or slightly higher (BMI 18.5 to 30)

Purging signs: Russell's sign, parotid enlargement, dental erosion, hypokalemia

Risk: esophageal tears, gastric rupture, dysrhythmias

cards.prompt: Binge eating disorder
cards.promptHtml: Binge eating disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: large intake in a short time, loss of control, distress, no compensatory behavior; at least weekly for 3 months

Facts: most common eating disorder; overweight/obese

Risks: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cancer

cards.prompt: Anorexia vs bulimia: findings that tell them apart
cards.promptHtml: Anorexia vs bulimia: findings that tell them apart
cards.answerHtml:
Anorexia: under 85% weight, lanugo, amenorrhea, low vitals

Bulimia: normal/slightly higher weight, Russell's sign, parotid swelling, dental erosion, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis with vomiting

Laxatives: metabolic acidosis, diarrhea

cards.prompt: Eating disorders: labs, electrolytes and organs affected
cards.promptHtml: Eating disorders: labs, electrolytes and organs affected
cards.answerHtml:
Electrolytes: hypokalemia (especially bulimia), hyponatremia, hypochloremia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia

Acid-base: alkalosis (vomiting), acidosis (laxatives)

Other: high BUN, low albumin, leukopenia, anemia, low estrogen/testosterone

Heart: prolonged QT, dysrhythmias, cardiomyopathy

Bone: osteoporosis

cards.prompt: Eating disorders: criteria for acute care admission
cards.promptHtml: Eating disorders: criteria for acute care admission
cards.answerHtml:
Admit for:

  • rapid weight loss or more than 30% in 6 months
  • HR below 40/min, systolic BP below 70, temp below 36 C (96.8 F)
  • ECG changes, electrolyte disturbance
  • failed outpatient gain or contract
  • severe depression, suicidal behavior, psychosis, family crisis

cards.prompt: Refeeding syndrome
cards.promptHtml: Refeeding syndrome
cards.answerHtml:
What: potentially fatal shift when fluids, electrolytes and carbohydrates are given to a severely malnourished client

Watch: dysrhythmias, severe bradycardia, hypotension

Nursing:

  • hospital setting, controlled feeding rate with dietitian
  • continuous cardiac monitoring, frequent VS
  • monitor electrolytes, give fluids as prescribed

cards.prompt: Nursing care and nutrition plan for eating disorders
cards.promptHtml: Nursing care and nutrition plan for eating disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Nursing:

  • structured milieu, consistent staff, behavioral contract, reward positive behavior
  • watch during and after meals (prevent purging)
  • weigh, I&O; 2 to 3 lb/week gain acceptable

Diet: structured schedule, small frequent meals, high fiber, low sodium, no caffeine

Avoid: "why" questions, talk about weight

cards.prompt: Fluoxetine (Prozac) for eating disorders
cards.promptHtml: Fluoxetine (Prozac) for eating disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI

Use: eating disorders (bulimia)

Monitor: response in 1 to 3 weeks; maximal up to 2 months

Teach: avoid driving/machinery until effects known; report intolerable sexual dysfunction

Stop & report: suicidality, serotonin syndrome (see Ch 22)

cards.prompt: Somatic symptom disorder
cards.promptHtml: Somatic symptom disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: physical symptoms without pathology, excessive preoccupation, usually over 6 months; many providers, high health use

Tool: PHQ-15

Nursing:

  • accept symptoms as real
  • limit symptom talk, encourage independence
  • report new physical symptoms
  • watch for suicidal ideation, analgesic/anxiolytic overuse

cards.prompt: Illness anxiety disorder
cards.promptHtml: Illness anxiety disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: fear of serious illness for over 6 months despite negative tests; minimal symptoms

Types: health-seeking, care-avoidant

Nursing: build trust, brief frequent visits, independence in self-care, support groups, stress management

Meds: antidepressants, anxiolytics

cards.prompt: Conversion disorder
cards.promptHtml: Conversion disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: neurologic symptoms (paralysis, blindness, aphonia, seizure-like) with no neurologic cause; triggered by stress

Clue: la belle indifference (lack of concern)

Course: about 95% remit; relapse about 20% within 1 year

Nursing: ensure safety, find the trigger, teach coping

cards.prompt: Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions
cards.promptHtml: Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: a confirmed medical diagnosis plus psychological/behavioral factors that worsen it, delay recovery or interfere with adherence

Nursing: discuss exam findings, explore fears, teach coping and assertiveness, watch for suicidal ideation, address physical and psychological needs

cards.prompt: Factitious disorder vs factitious disorder imposed on another
cards.promptHtml: Factitious disorder vs factitious disorder imposed on another
cards.answerHtml:
Factitious disorder: conscious falsification or self-injury, no external gain; wants attention; dramatic story, medical terms, new symptoms after negative tests

Imposed on another: harms a vulnerable person for attention

Nursing: avoid confrontation, share suspicions with team, protect victims

cards.prompt: Factitious disorder vs malingering
cards.promptHtml: Factitious disorder vs malingering
cards.answerHtml:
Factitious: conscious falsification for attention only; a mental illness

Malingering: conscious falsification for personal gain (disability benefits, avoiding military service); not a mental illness

Not conscious: somatic symptom and conversion disorders (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Reattribution treatment for somatic symptoms
cards.promptHtml: Reattribution treatment for somatic symptoms
cards.answerHtml:
4 stages:

  • feeling understood (listen, empathy, symptom history)
  • broadening the agenda (acknowledge concerns, give feedback)
  • making the link (no physical cause, protect self-esteem)
  • negotiating further treatment (regular follow-up)

Follow-up: visits every 4 to 6 weeks

cards.prompt: Somatic disorders: medications and teaching
cards.promptHtml: Somatic disorders: medications and teaching
cards.answerHtml:
Meds: analgesics, antidepressants, anxiolytics as prescribed (Ch 21–22)

Watch: overuse of analgesics and antianxiety drugs; substance use

Teach: individual/group therapy, stress management, assertiveness, daily exercise, support groups, follow-up every 4 to 6 weeks

cards.prompt: Alprazolam (Xanax)
cards.promptHtml: Alprazolam (Xanax)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: benzodiazepine (enhances GABA; Schedule IV)

Use: short-term GAD and panic disorder

Stop & report: anterograde amnesia (withhold), paradoxical rage/excitation; toxicity (drowsiness, confusion)

Teach: no alcohol or CNS depressants, no driving, swallow sustained-release whole

Contraindicated: sleep apnea, respiratory depression, glaucoma

Antidote: flumazenil

cards.prompt: Alprazolam toxicity: what does the nurse do first?
cards.promptHtml: Alprazolam toxicity: what does the nurse do first?
cards.answerHtml:
Order (ATI):

  • assess the client first (level of orientation)
  • monitor VS, keep airway patent, resuscitation equipment ready
  • IV fluids for blood pressure
  • give flumazenil to reverse sedation

Oral: drowsiness, confusion

IV benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam): respiratory depression, severe hypotension, cardiac arrest

cards.prompt: Alprazolam withdrawal and stopping the drug
cards.promptHtml: Alprazolam withdrawal and stopping the drug
cards.answerHtml:
Withdrawal: anxiety, insomnia, diaphoresis, tremors, lightheadedness, delirium, seizures

Nursing:

  • never stop abruptly
  • after long-term high-dose use, taper over several weeks
  • dependence can develop; report withdrawal signs
  • store securely (misuse potential)

Say: "Do not stop alprazolam suddenly. We will lower it slowly."

cards.prompt: Alprazolam: client reports memory gaps or sudden rage
cards.promptHtml: Alprazolam: client reports memory gaps or sudden rage
cards.answerHtml:
Anterograde amnesia: trouble recalling events after the dose; withhold the drug and notify the provider

Paradoxical response: insomnia, excitation, euphoria, anxiety, rage; notify the provider

Not paradoxical: sedation or respiratory depression with alcohol/opioids is expected CNS depression

cards.prompt: Buspirone (BuSpar)
cards.promptHtml: Buspirone (BuSpar)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: atypical antianxiety (serotonin/dopamine receptors)

Use: GAD only; no sedation, no misuse risk

Monitor: dizziness, nausea, headache

Teach: daily on schedule, not PRN; starts in 1 week, full effect takes several weeks; avoid grapefruit juice, erythromycin, ketoconazole

Contraindicated: MAOIs or within 14 days after (hypertensive crisis)

cards.prompt: Client on buspirone says "I will take it only when I feel anxious." Response?
cards.promptHtml: Client on buspirone says "I will take it only when I feel anxious." Response?
cards.answerHtml:
Say: "Buspirone takes a week or more to start working, so keep taking it every day."

Why: slow onset; schedule dosing, not PRN

Timeline: 1 week to start, several weeks for full effect (ATI gives 2–6, up to 4, and 3–6 weeks)

cards.prompt: Paroxetine (Paxil)
cards.promptHtml: Paroxetine (Paxil)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor)

Use: GAD, panic, OCD, social anxiety, PTSD, depression

Monitor: baseline sodium then periodic (hyponatremia, older adults on diuretics); PT/INR with warfarin; weight

Stop & report: serotonin syndrome, bleeding, suicidality

Teach: morning dose, daily, up to 4 weeks for effect

Taper: do not stop abruptly

cards.prompt: Serotonin syndrome: onset, signs and nursing action
cards.promptHtml: Serotonin syndrome: onset, signs and nursing action
cards.answerHtml:
Onset: 2 to 72 hr after starting; can be lethal

Looks like: confusion, agitation, hallucinations, tachycardia, labile BP, diaphoresis, fever, hyperreflexia, incoordination, diarrhea, seizures, coma

Nursing: withhold the next dose, notify the provider

Cause: SSRI or SNRI with MAOIs, TCAs, St. John's wort

cards.prompt: Paroxetine or venlafaxine stopped abruptly: what happens?
cards.promptHtml: Paroxetine or venlafaxine stopped abruptly: what happens?
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: nausea, sensory disturbances, anxiety, tremor, malaise

Prevent: never stop abruptly; taper slowly after long use

Teach: take daily; do not change dose without prescriber

cards.prompt: Paroxetine plus phenelzine, warfarin, NSAIDs or lithium: what happens?
cards.promptHtml: Paroxetine plus phenelzine, warfarin, NSAIDs or lithium: what happens?
cards.answerHtml:
MAOI/St. John's wort/TCA: serotonin syndrome

Washout: stop MAOI 14 days before SSRI; stop fluoxetine 5 weeks before an MAOI

Warfarin: higher warfarin levels; monitor PT/INR and bleeding

NSAIDs/anticoagulants: bleeding (bruising, hematuria)

TCAs/lithium: levels rise; avoid

cards.prompt: Venlafaxine (Effexor)
cards.promptHtml: Venlafaxine (Effexor)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SNRI (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor)

Use: major depression, panic, GAD

Monitor: blood pressure (hypertension), weight loss, sodium (older adults on diuretics)

Stop & report: serotonin syndrome, suicidal thoughts

Contraindicated: MAOIs; stop MAOI 14 days before

Teach: avoid abrupt cessation, avoid alcohol, up to 4 weeks for effect

cards.prompt: Paroxetine bruxism and sexual dysfunction: what helps?
cards.promptHtml: Paroxetine bruxism and sexual dysfunction: what helps?
cards.answerHtml:
Bruxism: mouth guard at night; report; switch class or add low-dose buspirone

Sexual dysfunction (late, after 5 to 6 weeks): dose reduction, medication holiday, or change medications

Other late effects: weight gain, headache

cards.prompt: Sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, fluvoxamine: uses
cards.promptHtml: Sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, fluvoxamine: uses
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRIs (like paroxetine and fluoxetine)

Sertraline: panic, OCD, social anxiety, PTSD

Citalopram: panic, OCD, GAD, PTSD, social anxiety

Escitalopram: GAD, OCD, panic, PTSD, social anxiety

Fluvoxamine: OCD, GAD, social anxiety, PTSD

First-line for panic and trauma/stressor disorders

cards.prompt: Propranolol, prazosin, clonidine for trauma-related disorders
cards.promptHtml: Propranolol, prazosin, clonidine for trauma-related disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Class: propranolol is a beta blocker; prazosin a peripheral alpha blocker; clonidine a central alpha-2 agonist

Use: listed by ATI for trauma- and stressor-related disorders

Note: ATI gives names only, no detailed content

cards.prompt: Hydroxyzine, mirtazapine, trazodone, gabapentin, pregabalin: ATI anxiety coverage
cards.promptHtml: Hydroxyzine, mirtazapine, trazodone, gabapentin, pregabalin: ATI anxiety coverage
cards.answerHtml:
Class: other agents ATI lists for anxiety/trauma (with TCAs and the MAOI phenelzine)

Note: ATI names them only; no detail in this chapter

Mirtazapine, trazodone: see Ch 22

cards.prompt: Amitriptyline (Elavil)
cards.promptHtml: Amitriptyline (Elavil)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: TCA (blocks norepinephrine/serotonin reuptake)

Use: depression; also neuropathic pain, insomnia

Monitor: baseline ECG, VS, orthostatic BP/HR

Stop & report: dysrhythmia, confusion, seizures; hold dose for significant orthostatic drop

Teach: bedtime dose, sunglasses, fluids 2–3 L/day, sugarless gum, 10–14 days or longer to start

Contraindicated: seizure disorders

cards.prompt: Amitriptyline overdose: why limit supply?
cards.promptHtml: Amitriptyline overdose: why limit supply?
cards.answerHtml:
Why: high lethality in overdose and suicide risk

Toxicity: cholinergic blockade and cardiac toxicity: dysrhythmia, confusion, agitation, then seizures, coma, death

Nursing: no more than a 1-week supply for acutely ill clients; baseline ECG; frequent vital signs

cards.prompt: Fluoxetine (Prozac)
cards.promptHtml: Fluoxetine (Prozac)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI

Use: depression, OCD, bulimia, PMDD, panic, PTSD

Monitor: sodium (older adults on diuretics), PT/INR with warfarin, weight

Stop & report: serotonin syndrome (2–72 hr), rash, GI bleeding

Teach: morning dose, avoid caffeine; mouth guard for bruxism

Taper: gradually (headache, nausea, tremor if abrupt)

Washout: stop 5 weeks before an MAOI

cards.prompt: Phenelzine (Nardil)
cards.promptHtml: Phenelzine (Nardil)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: MAOI

Use: depression (first-line for atypical depression), panic, social anxiety, PTSD

Monitor: BP, orthostatic changes

Stop & report: hypertensive crisis, hypomania/mania

Teach: strict tyramine diet in writing; no OTC drugs without approval

Contraindicated: SSRIs, heart failure, cardiovascular disease, pheochromocytoma

Avoid: meperidine (hyperpyrexia), decongestants

cards.prompt: Phenelzine hypertensive crisis: signs and treatment
cards.promptHtml: Phenelzine hypertensive crisis: signs and treatment
cards.answerHtml:
Cause: dietary tyramine or sympathomimetics (decongestants, amphetamine) or TCAs

Looks like: headache, N/V, rapid HR, severe hypertension, diaphoresis, changed LOC

Nursing: assist RN with phentolamine IV or nifedipine, continuous cardiac monitoring, respiratory support

cards.prompt: Phenelzine diet: foods and drugs to avoid
cards.promptHtml: Phenelzine diet: foods and drugs to avoid
cards.answerHtml:
Avoid: aged cheese, pepperoni, salami, avocado, figs, bananas, smoked fish, some beer, red wine

Also: caffeine, chocolate, fava beans, ginseng, decongestants, other OTC drugs

Teach: give written lists; check ability to follow strict diet

Surgery: not within 10 to 14 days before or after general anesthesia

cards.prompt: Bupropion (Wellbutrin)
cards.promptHtml: Bupropion (Wellbutrin)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: atypical antidepressant (inhibits dopamine uptake)

Use: depression, smoking cessation, seasonal depression; alternative when SSRI sexual dysfunction

Monitor: food intake and weight

Stop & report: seizures (higher doses)

Contraindicated: seizure disorder, anorexia/bulimia, MAOIs, head injury risk

Washout: stop MAOI 2 weeks before

Teach: 1 to 3 weeks to feel effect; full effect 2 to 3 months

cards.prompt: Mirtazapine (Remeron)
cards.promptHtml: Mirtazapine (Remeron)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: atypical antidepressant (increases release of serotonin and norepinephrine)

Use: depression; effects sooner and less sexual dysfunction than SSRIs

Monitor: weight, cholesterol

Teach: sleepiness (worse with other CNS depressants), increased appetite and weight gain

cards.prompt: Trazodone (Desyrel) and vilazodone (Viibryd)
cards.promptHtml: Trazodone (Desyrel) and vilazodone (Viibryd)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: atypical antidepressants (serotonin receptor blockade; vilazodone also reuptake block)

Trazodone: bedtime; helps SSRI insomnia; caution in cardiac disease. Priapism: seek care immediately

Vilazodone: give with food; monitor sodium; stop and report serotonin syndrome or NMS signs

cards.prompt: Duloxetine (Cymbalta), desvenlafaxine, levomilnacipran
cards.promptHtml: Duloxetine (Cymbalta), desvenlafaxine, levomilnacipran
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SNRI (serotonin and norepinephrine)

Prototype: venlafaxine (Ch 21)

Monitor: sodium (older adults), weight loss, blood pressure

Contraindicated: duloxetine with hepatic disease or heavy alcohol use

Teach: never stop abruptly, discuss sexual dysfunction

cards.prompt: Fluoxetine, amitriptyline and suicide risk: who and what to do
cards.promptHtml: Fluoxetine, amitriptyline and suicide risk: who and what to do
cards.answerHtml:
Who: highest in clients under 25; risk can rise early because energy returns before mood lifts

Nursing: ask directly about suicidal thoughts, suicide precautions until peak effect

Supply: 1 week for acutely ill, then 1 month at a time (especially TCAs)

cards.prompt: Serotonin syndrome: treatment and prevention
cards.promptHtml: Serotonin syndrome: treatment and prevention
cards.answerHtml:
Nursing: withhold the drug, notify provider

Treatment: serotonin blockade and muscle relaxants, cooling blankets, anticonvulsants, artificial ventilation

Prevent: never combine MAOI with SSRI/TCA; stop MAOI 14 days before an SSRI; stop fluoxetine 5 weeks before an MAOI

cards.prompt: Amitriptyline or phenelzine with a significant orthostatic drop: what does the nurse do?
cards.promptHtml: Amitriptyline or phenelzine with a significant orthostatic drop: what does the nurse do?
cards.answerHtml:
Do: check BP and pulse lying and standing

If significant BP drop or HR rise: do not give the drug; notify charge nurse and provider

Teach: change positions slowly, avoid dehydration, sit or lie down if dizzy

cards.prompt: Client on fluoxetine says "I don't feel better yet." Response?
cards.promptHtml: Client on fluoxetine says "I don't feel better yet." Response?
cards.answerHtml:
Say: "It can take several weeks to feel the full benefit, so please keep taking it daily."

Timing: TCAs 10–14 days to start, up to 4–8 weeks; bupropion 1–3 weeks

Don't: promise relief in a few days

Taper: never stop abruptly

cards.prompt: Lithium (Lithobid)
cards.promptHtml: Lithium (Lithobid)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: mood stabilizer (narrow therapeutic range)

Use: acute mania, prevents mania/depression, lowers suicide

Monitor: level 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L (draw 10–12 hr after last dose, morning); BUN/creatinine; TSH, T3, T4 annually; sodium

Stop & report: diarrhea, vomiting, sweating, rising tremor

Teach: 1.5–3 L fluid/day, normal salt, give with food

Contraindicated: severe renal/cardiac disease, hypovolemia

cards.prompt: Lithium level 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L: what does it mean and how often is it checked?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium level 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L: what does it mean and how often is it checked?
cards.answerHtml:
Meaning: maintenance range

Acute mania: higher needed (ATI text 1 to 1.5; answer key 0.8 to 1.4); 1.2 is expected, so give next dose

Draw: morning, 10 to 12 hr after last dose

Frequency: every 2 to 3 days at start until stable, then every 1 to 3 months; more often in older adults

cards.prompt: Lithium level less than 1.5 mEq/L: what does the nurse see and do?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium level less than 1.5 mEq/L: what does the nurse see and do?
cards.answerHtml:
Mild toxicity: diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, thirst, polyuria, muscle weakness, fine hand tremors, slurred speech, lethargy

Nursing: teach that findings at low levels often improve over time

But: if diarrhea, vomiting or excessive sweating, withhold lithium and seek care

cards.prompt: Lithium level 1.5 to 2.0 mEq/L: what does the nurse see and do?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium level 1.5 to 2.0 mEq/L: what does the nurse see and do?
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: confusion, sedation, poor coordination, coarse tremors, ongoing GI distress

Nursing: withhold lithium, notify provider; new dose based on lithium and sodium levels; promote excretion

cards.prompt: Lithium level 2.0 to 2.5 mEq/L: what does the nurse see and do?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium level 2.0 to 2.5 mEq/L: what does the nurse see and do?
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: extreme dilute polyuria, tinnitus, blurred vision, ataxia, jerking, seizures, severe hypotension, stupor to coma

Treat: acute care; emetic if alert or gastric lavage; urea, mannitol or aminophylline to increase excretion

Risk: death from respiratory complications

cards.prompt: Lithium level above 2.5 mEq/L: what does the nurse see and do?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium level above 2.5 mEq/L: what does the nurse see and do?
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: rapid progression to coma and death

Treat: acute care setting with supportive measures; hemodialysis can be warranted

cards.prompt: Lithium interactions: furosemide, ibuprofen, diphenhydramine
cards.promptHtml: Lithium interactions: furosemide, ibuprofen, diphenhydramine
cards.answerHtml:
Diuretics: sodium loss lowers lithium excretion, toxicity; avoid or monitor closely

NSAIDs: raise lithium reabsorption, toxicity; avoid, use aspirin for mild pain

Anticholinergics (antihistamines, TCAs): urinary retention and abdominal discomfort; avoid

Teach: keep salt and fluid steady

cards.prompt: Lithium side effects and their treatments
cards.promptHtml: Lithium side effects and their treatments
cards.answerHtml:
Fine tremor: propranolol, lowest/divided/long-acting dose; report increased tremor

Polyuria/thirst: spironolactone, fluids

GI upset: give with food

Goiter/hypothyroidism: levothyroxine; teach cold, dry skin, bradycardia, weight gain

Renal toxicity: I&O, BUN/creatinine

cards.prompt: Carbamazepine (Tegretol)
cards.promptHtml: Carbamazepine (Tegretol)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: anticonvulsant used as mood stabilizer

Use: mixed mania, rapid cycling

Monitor: level 4 to 12 mcg/mL; CBC/platelets; sodium (hypoosmolarity)

Stop & report: rash or Stevens-Johnson, bruising, infection signs

Teach: bedtime, sunscreen, no grapefruit juice; lowers effect of oral contraceptives and warfarin

Contraindicated: bone marrow suppression

cards.prompt: Valproate (Depakote)
cards.promptHtml: Valproate (Depakote)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: anticonvulsant used as mood stabilizer

Use: mixed mania, rapid cycling

Monitor: level 50 to 120 mcg/mL; LFTs at least every 2 months for first 6 months; amylase; platelets

Stop & report: hepatotoxicity (jaundice, anorexia, abdominal pain), pancreatitis (stop drug), bruising

Teach: with food; weight gain; avoid in children under 2

cards.prompt: Lamotrigine (Lamictal)
cards.promptHtml: Lamotrigine (Lamictal)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: anticonvulsant used as mood stabilizer

Stop & report: any serious rash (Stevens-Johnson); withhold and notify

Teach: slow titration lowers rash risk; blurred vision, dizziness

Interactions: valproate raises levels; carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital lower them; oral contraceptives less effective

cards.prompt: Stevens-Johnson syndrome with carbamazepine or lamotrigine
cards.promptHtml: Stevens-Johnson syndrome with carbamazepine or lamotrigine
cards.answerHtml:
What: serious skin reaction (carbamazepine, lamotrigine)

Nursing: withhold the drug, notify provider immediately; report any rash

Mild rash: anti-inflammatory/antihistamine

Teach: sunscreen

cards.prompt: Bipolar adjuncts: olanzapine, quetiapine, lurasidone, clonazepam, bupropion
cards.promptHtml: Bipolar adjuncts: olanzapine, quetiapine, lurasidone, clonazepam, bupropion
cards.answerHtml:
Class: adjuncts to lithium/valproate

Antipsychotics (olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, ziprasidone): acute mania; lurasidone approved for bipolar depression

Clonazepam, lorazepam: acute mania and agitation

Bupropion, venlafaxine, SSRIs: depression only with a mood stabilizer (prevents rebound mania)

cards.prompt: Chlorpromazine (Thorazine)
cards.promptHtml: Chlorpromazine (Thorazine)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: first-generation antipsychotic, low potency (blocks D2)

Use: psychosis, mania, nausea/vomiting, agitation

Monitor: CBC if infection signs; baseline ECG and potassium; LFTs

Stop & report: NMS, WBC under 3,000, jaundice

Teach: sedation and anticholinergic effects high, EPS low; bedtime dose; sunscreen

Contraindicated: coma, Parkinson's, dementia in older adults

cards.prompt: Haloperidol (Haldol)
cards.promptHtml: Haloperidol (Haldol)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: first-generation antipsychotic, high potency

Use: psychosis, Tourette, agitation

Monitor: EPS with AIMS

Teach: high EPS, low sedation, low anticholinergic effects

Taper/adherence: haloperidol or fluphenazine decanoate IM every 2 to 4 weeks for nonadherence; not addictive but do not stop abruptly

cards.prompt: Chlorpromazine vs haloperidol: sedation, dry mouth and EPS
cards.promptHtml: Chlorpromazine vs haloperidol: sedation, dry mouth and EPS
cards.answerHtml:
Low potency (chlorpromazine): low EPS, high sedation, high anticholinergic

Medium (loxapine, perphenazine): moderate on all

High potency (haloperidol, fluphenazine, thiothixene): high EPS, low sedation, low anticholinergic

cards.prompt: Acute dystonia: timing, signs and treatment
cards.promptHtml: Acute dystonia: timing, signs and treatment
cards.answerHtml:
Timing: 1 to 5 days after first dose

Looks like: severe spasm of tongue, neck, face, back; airway risk

Nursing: stay with the client, monitor airway

Treat: IM/IV benztropine or diphenhydramine

Course: spasms usually subside in 5 to 15 min

cards.prompt: Pseudoparkinsonism (EPS)
cards.promptHtml: Pseudoparkinsonism (EPS)
cards.answerHtml:
Timing: 5 to 30 days after first dose; watch first month

Looks like: bradykinesia, rigidity, shuffling gait, drooling, pill-rolling tremor, mask-like face

Treat: benztropine or trihexyphenidyl

Nursing: fall precautions

cards.prompt: Akathisia (EPS)
cards.promptHtml: Akathisia (EPS)
cards.answerHtml:
Timing: 5 to 60 days after first dose; watch first 2 months

Looks like: cannot sit or stand still, continual pacing, agitation

Treat: antiparkinsonian drug, beta blocker, or lorazepam/diazepam

Watch: suicide risk with severe akathisia

cards.prompt: Tardive dyskinesia
cards.promptHtml: Tardive dyskinesia
cards.answerHtml:
Timing: months to years; evaluate after 12 months of therapy, then every 3 months

Looks like: lip smacking, tongue movements, involuntary arm/leg/trunk movements

Nursing: AIMS; lower dose or switch to a second-generation drug

Key: usually does not improve even after stopping; no reliable treatment

cards.prompt: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
cards.promptHtml: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: sudden high fever, muscle rigidity, BP swings, diaphoresis, tachycardia, decreased LOC

Timing: first week or any time

Nursing: stop the drug, cooling blankets, antipyretics, fluids, ICU

Drugs: dantrolene or bromocriptine

Restart: wait 2 weeks; consider an atypical

cards.prompt: Clozapine (Clozaril)
cards.promptHtml: Clozapine (Clozaril)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: second-generation antipsychotic (not first-line)

Monitor: WBC weekly, biweekly, then monthly; glucose, lipids, weight

Stop & report: fever, sore throat, mouth lesions (agranulocytosis, usually first 6 months, gradual onset)

Teach: hypersalivation, sedation, orthostasis, highest anticholinergic effect

Avoid: immunosuppressives (anticancer drugs)

cards.prompt: Risperidone (Risperdal)
cards.promptHtml: Risperidone (Risperdal)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: second-generation antipsychotic (prototype)

Use: positive and negative symptoms, fewer EPS

Monitor: baseline and periodic fasting glucose, weight; prolactin effects

Stop & report: increased thirst/urination/appetite (metabolic syndrome), EPS

Teach: depot IM every 2 weeks, effect 2 to 6 weeks after first injection; ODT for cheeking

Contraindicated: dementia

cards.prompt: Asenapine (Saphris), lurasidone (Latuda), ziprasidone (Geodon): administration
cards.promptHtml: Asenapine (Saphris), lurasidone (Latuda), ziprasidone (Geodon): administration
cards.answerHtml:
Class: second-generation antipsychotics

Asenapine: sublingual, do not swallow, no food or drink for 10 min

Lurasidone: with food, at least 350 kcal

Ziprasidone: with food; ECG/QT prolongation, torsades

Avoid: combining with QT-prolonging drugs (TCAs, amiodarone, clarithromycin)

cards.prompt: Olanzapine (Zyprexa), quetiapine (Seroquel), paliperidone (Invega), iloperidone (Fanapt)
cards.promptHtml: Olanzapine (Zyprexa), quetiapine (Seroquel), paliperidone (Invega), iloperidone (Fanapt)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: second-generation antipsychotics

Olanzapine: high risk diabetes/weight gain; observe at least 3 hr after ER injection

Quetiapine: moderate metabolic risk, cataracts

Paliperidone: metabolic risk, prolonged QT; ER injection every 28 days, Trinza every 3 months

Iloperidone: weight gain, QT, orthostasis; follow titration

cards.prompt: Aripiprazole (Abilify)
cards.promptHtml: Aripiprazole (Abilify)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: third-generation antipsychotic (dopamine partial agonist/antagonist)

Use: positive and negative symptoms, bipolar

Monitor: low risk of EPS, weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia, orthostasis, anticholinergic effects

Teach: sedation, headache, insomnia, GI upset; monthly LAI

Interactions: barbiturates/phenytoin lower levels; fluconazole raises them

cards.prompt: Agranulocytosis: chlorpromazine and clozapine WBC limits
cards.promptHtml: Agranulocytosis: chlorpromazine and clozapine WBC limits
cards.answerHtml:
Signs: fever, sore throat, mouth lesions

Action: CBC if infection signs; first-generation drugs (chlorpromazine) stopped if WBC under 3,000/mm3

Timing: gradual, usually first 6 months (clozapine; chlorpromazine too)

Clozapine: WBC per protocol (weekly, biweekly, then monthly)

cards.prompt: Metabolic syndrome from risperidone, olanzapine, clozapine
cards.promptHtml: Metabolic syndrome from risperidone, olanzapine, clozapine
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: weight gain, new diabetes or glucose loss, dyslipidemia, hypertension

Monitor: baseline fasting glucose and periodic; cholesterol, triglycerides, glucose if gain over 14 kg (31 lb)

Highest risk: clozapine, olanzapine

Teach: diet, exercise, report thirst, urination, appetite

cards.prompt: Methylphenidate (Ritalin)
cards.promptHtml: Methylphenidate (Ritalin)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: CNS stimulant (raises norepinephrine and dopamine); other amphetamine-type drugs same family

Use: ADHD; does not cure it, pair with family and cognitive therapy

Monitor:

  • height and weight (growth suppression; ask provider about a medication holiday)
  • VS and ECG (sudden death risk with heart abnormalities)

Teach:

  • last dose before 4 p.m.; tablets 30-45 min before meals
  • swallow sustained-release whole
  • no caffeine or alcohol
  • controlled substance: lock up

cards.prompt: Methylphenidate: hallucinations, patch rash, or toxicity. What does the nurse do?
cards.promptHtml: Methylphenidate: hallucinations, patch rash, or toxicity. What does the nurse do?
cards.answerHtml:
Hallucinations or paranoia: report immediately and the drug is discontinued

Hives or papules from the patch: remove it and notify the provider

Toxicity (dizziness, palpitations, hypertension, hallucinations, seizures):

  • hallucinations: chlorpromazine
  • seizures: diazepam
  • give fluids

Abrupt stop: withdrawal (headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness, depression), so taper

Interaction: MAOI = hypertensive crisis; wait at least 14 days

cards.prompt: Atomoxetine (Strattera)
cards.promptHtml: Atomoxetine (Strattera)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SNRI; blocks norepinephrine reuptake; not a stimulant

Use: ADHD in children and adults

Monitor: height and weight; depression and mood

Stop & report:

  • suicidal ideation (mood change, agitation, irritability, excess sleep)
  • liver injury: yellow skin, abdominal pain, flu-like illness

Teach:

  • with food if GI upset; last dose before 4 p.m.
  • full effect up to 6 weeks
  • avoid with angle-closure glaucoma, pheochromocytoma, MAOIs (wait 14 days)

cards.prompt: Desipramine (Norpramin)
cards.promptHtml: Desipramine (Norpramin)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: TCA; blocks norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake

Use: depression, ADHD, autism spectrum, panic, separation anxiety, social phobia, OCD

Monitor: baseline ECG, frequent VS, BP with first dose (orthostasis)

Stop & report: irregular pulse, confusion, agitation, seizures

Teach:

  • bedtime dosing (sedation)
  • sugarless gum, sips of water, fluids 2-3 L/day for anticholinergic effects
  • initial effect 1-3 weeks, full about 6 weeks
  • do not stop suddenly (relapse)

Avoid: recent MI, heart failure, prolonged QT

cards.prompt: Desipramine: toxicity signs vs expected side effects
cards.promptHtml: Desipramine: toxicity signs vs expected side effects
cards.answerHtml:
Toxicity (cholinergic blockade and cardiac):

  • dysrhythmias, irregular pulse
  • confusion, agitation
  • then seizures, coma, death

Nursing: baseline ECG, frequent VS, report toxicity; 1-week supply if acutely ill (lethal in excess)

Not toxicity: dry mouth and photophobia are expected anticholinergic effects

Avoid: epinephrine and dopamine (hypertensive effect)

cards.prompt: Guanfacine (Intuniv)
cards.promptHtml: Guanfacine (Intuniv)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: alpha2-adrenergic agonist (other: clonidine)

Use: ADHD, tic disorders, conduct and oppositional defiant disorder

Monitor: BP and pulse at baseline, early treatment, and each dose change (hypotension, bradycardia)

Stop & report: never stop abruptly: rebound hypertension; taper by schedule

Teach:

  • sedation: avoid hazardous activities
  • no alcohol or other CNS depressants
  • avoid high-fat meals (raise absorption)
  • swallow extended-release whole
  • safety not established under age 6

cards.prompt: Risperidone (Risperdal) in children and adolescents
cards.promptHtml: Risperidone (Risperdal) in children and adolescents
cards.answerHtml:
Class: atypical antipsychotic (blocks serotonin mainly, dopamine less)

Use: autism spectrum, conduct disorder, OCD, psychotic symptoms

Monitor:

  • baseline fasting glucose, then periodically
  • cholesterol, triglycerides, glucose if weight gain over 14 kg (30 lb)
  • BP with first dose; EPS

Stop & report: thirst, urination, hunger (new diabetes); EPS

Teach: slow position changes, healthy diet and exercise, no alcohol, start low and go slow

cards.prompt: Fluoxetine (Prozac) in children and adolescents
cards.promptHtml: Fluoxetine (Prozac) in children and adolescents
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI; blocks serotonin reuptake

Use: MDD, OCD, GAD, bulimia, autism spectrum, IED

Stop & report:

  • suicidal thoughts (increased risk in children and teens)
  • agitation and hallucinations: possible serotonin syndrome

Teach:

  • take in the morning
  • response in 1-3 weeks, maximum by 12 weeks
  • avoid MAOIs, SNRIs, buspirone, St. John's wort; 2-5 weeks between fluoxetine and an MAOI (Ch 22: stop fluoxetine 5 weeks before)

Taper/withdrawal: abrupt stop causes discontinuation syndrome (dizziness, insomnia, irritability, agitation)

cards.prompt: Which child and adolescent drugs raise suicide risk, and what do parents report?
cards.promptHtml: Which child and adolescent drugs raise suicide risk, and what do parents report?
cards.answerHtml:
Raise suicidal ideation in youth:

  • SSRIs
  • TCAs
  • atomoxetine

Parents report:

  • mood changes
  • excessive sleeping
  • agitation
  • irritability
  • any suicidal talk

Nursing: safety first; limit TCA supply (1 week if acutely ill); monitor for depression

cards.prompt: Abruptly stopping child and adolescent psychiatric drugs: what happens with each?
cards.promptHtml: Abruptly stopping child and adolescent psychiatric drugs: what happens with each?
cards.answerHtml:
Stimulants: withdrawal (headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness, depression)

Guanfacine/clonidine: rebound hypertension; taper

SSRIs: discontinuation syndrome (dizziness, insomnia, nervousness, irritability, agitation); taper

TCAs: relapse

Teach: daily dosing builds therapeutic levels; keep taking after improvement; never stop without the provider

cards.prompt: Alcohol withdrawal vs opioid withdrawal
cards.promptHtml: Alcohol withdrawal vs opioid withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Alcohol:

  • starts 4-12 hr after last drink, lasts 5-7 days
  • tremors, nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, high HR/BP/RR/temp, seizures
  • delirium at 2-3 days: medical emergency, can be fatal

Opioid:

  • hours to several days
  • agitation, flu-like symptoms, runny nose, yawning, dilated pupils, diarrhea, goose bumps
  • not life-threatening, but suicidal ideation can occur

Nursing: baseline and ongoing VS, neuro checks, seizure precautions

cards.prompt: Chlordiazepoxide (Librium) and lorazepam (Ativan) in alcohol withdrawal
cards.promptHtml: Chlordiazepoxide (Librium) and lorazepam (Ativan) in alcohol withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Class: benzodiazepines (cross-tolerant substitution therapy; diazepam and oxazepam too)

Use: alcohol withdrawal: keep VS in range, decrease seizure risk and withdrawal intensity

Monitor: baseline and ongoing VS and neuro status

Teach/nursing:

  • give around the clock or PRN as prescribed
  • seizure precautions
  • short-term use only

Antidote: flumazenil reverses toxicity (sedation)

cards.prompt: Disulfiram (Antabuse)
cards.promptHtml: Disulfiram (Antabuse)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: aversion therapy for alcohol use disorder

Use: daily oral; any alcohol causes acetaldehyde syndrome

Monitor: liver function tests (hepatotoxicity)

Stop & report: reaction: nausea, vomiting, weakness, sweating, palpitations, hypotension; can progress to respiratory depression, seizures, death

Teach:

  • first dose 12 hr after last drink
  • avoid hidden alcohol: cough syrup, aftershave, mouthwash, hand sanitizer
  • medical alert bracelet
  • reaction risk lasts 2 weeks after stopping
  • join a self-help program

cards.prompt: Naltrexone (Vivitrol)
cards.promptHtml: Naltrexone (Vivitrol)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: pure opioid antagonist

Use: prevents relapse in alcohol and opioid use disorder; blocks craving and the pleasurable effects

Monitor: screen for opioid dependence first (risk of precipitated withdrawal and opioid toxicity)

Teach:

  • oral daily with meals for GI upset, or monthly IM depot if adherence is poor
  • heroin use while taking it can cause withdrawal and death
  • join a 12-step program

cards.prompt: Acamprosate (Campral)
cards.promptHtml: Acamprosate (Campral)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: abstinence maintenance for alcohol use disorder

Use: reduces dysphoria, anxiety, and restlessness of abstinence

Teach:

  • oral, three times a day
  • diarrhea is the adverse effect: keep up fluids
  • join a self-help program

Avoid: kidney impairment

cards.prompt: Methadone vs buprenorphine (Suboxone)
cards.promptHtml: Methadone vs buprenorphine (Suboxone)
cards.answerHtml:
Methadone:

  • opioid agonist substitution; prevents abstinence syndrome, used for withdrawal and maintenance
  • only from an approved treatment center
  • slow taper to detoxify

Buprenorphine:

  • agonist-antagonist, schedule III; decreases craving
  • sublingual tablet, buccal film, or skin implant
  • a primary care provider can prescribe and dispense

Both: encourage a 12-step program

cards.prompt: Naloxone (Narcan) vs flumazenil (Romazicon)
cards.promptHtml: Naloxone (Narcan) vs flumazenil (Romazicon)
cards.answerHtml:
Naloxone:

  • Class: opioid antagonist
  • Use: opioid overdose: reverses respiratory depression and coma
  • routes: IM, SQ, IV, inhalation

Flumazenil:

  • Class: competitive benzodiazepine receptor antagonist
  • Use: reverses benzodiazepine sedation and toxicity
  • IV

Remember: opioid toxicity = naloxone; benzodiazepine toxicity = flumazenil

cards.prompt: Clonidine (Catapres) and propranolol (Inderal) in withdrawal
cards.promptHtml: Clonidine (Catapres) and propranolol (Inderal) in withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Class: clonidine is an alpha2 agonist; propranolol and atenolol are beta blockers

Use: depress the autonomic response (lower BP and HR); clonidine treats opioid withdrawal symptoms but not craving; propranolol and atenolol also reduce craving

Monitor: baseline and ongoing VS

Stop & report: hold beta blocker if HR is below 50/min

Teach: clonidine drowsiness (avoid hazardous tasks), dry mouth: sugarless gum, sips of water

Also: carbamazepine decreases withdrawal seizures

cards.prompt: Nicotine replacement products: key teaching
cards.promptHtml: Nicotine replacement products: key teaching
cards.answerHtml:
Class: nicotine replacement; nearly doubles cessation rate; never combine nicotine products

Gum: chew slowly over 30 min; nothing by mouth 15 min before or during; not beyond 6 months

Patch: morning on, off at bedtime (16 hr); remove before MRI

Lozenge: nothing by mouth 15 min before or during; dissolves over 20-30 min; max 5 per 6 hr or 20/day

Spray/inhaler: avoid in asthma and chronic sinus problems; inhaler taper over 2-3 months

cards.prompt: Varenicline (Chantix) and bupropion (Zyban)
cards.promptHtml: Varenicline (Chantix) and bupropion (Zyban)
cards.answerHtml:
Varenicline class: nicotinic receptor agonist; reduces craving and withdrawal

Monitor: BP; glucose control in diabetes

Stop & report: new depression, suicidal thoughts, unpredictable behavior, chest pain

Teach: take after a meal; nausea is common

Occupation: banned for truck/bus drivers, air traffic controllers, pilots

Bupropion: decreases nicotine craving; relieve dry mouth; avoid caffeine and other CNS stimulants (insomnia)

cards.prompt: Kübler-Ross stages of grief
cards.promptHtml: Kübler-Ross stages of grief
cards.answerHtml:
1 Denial: cannot believe the loss

2 Anger: at self, others, objects

3 Bargaining: negotiates for time or a cure

4 Depression: overwhelming sadness

5 Acceptance: accepts and plans ahead

Remember: clients do not always move in order; time needed varies

cards.prompt: Bowlby vs Engel stages of grief
cards.promptHtml: Bowlby vs Engel stages of grief
cards.answerHtml:
Bowlby (4): numbness/protest, disequilibrium, disorganization and despair, reorganization (seen as early as 6 months of age)

Engel (5):

  • shock and disbelief
  • developing awareness (begins within hours)
  • restitution (rituals, funeral)
  • resolution (preoccupation fades over about 12 months)
  • recovery

cards.prompt: Worden's four tasks of mourning
cards.promptHtml: Worden's four tasks of mourning
cards.answerHtml:
I: accept the reality of the loss

II: process the pain of grief

III: adjust to a world without the lost person

IV: find an enduring connection while starting a new life

cards.prompt: Normal vs complicated grief
cards.promptHtml: Normal vs complicated grief
cards.answerHtml:
Normal:

  • crying, anger, guilt, withdrawal, somatic symptoms (chest pain, palpitations, headache, fatigue)
  • some acceptance by 6 months

Complicated:

  • delayed/inhibited, distorted/exaggerated, or chronic/prolonged
  • loss of self-esteem and worthlessness; cannot do ADLs
  • suicidal thoughts: monitor

Risk factors: unexpected, violent, or young death; dependence on the deceased; poor support; prior depression or substance use

Refer: psychotherapy for maladaptive grief

cards.prompt: Types of loss and disenfranchised grief
cards.promptHtml: Types of loss and disenfranchised grief
cards.answerHtml:
Necessary: part of life's cycle

Actual: any valued person or item

Perceived: defined by the client, not obvious to others

Maturational: expected developmental loss

Situational: unanticipated, external event

Disenfranchised grief: cannot be shared publicly or is not accepted (suicide, abortion)

Anticipatory grief: "letting go" before an expected loss

cards.prompt: Grieving client: what should the nurse say and avoid?
cards.promptHtml: Grieving client: what should the nurse say and avoid?
cards.answerHtml:
Do:

  • name the emotion ("You sound angry. Anger is normal after a loss. Tell me how you are feeling.")
  • use silence and presence
  • encourage sharing memories

Avoid:

  • cliches ("They are in a better place")
  • false reassurance
  • giving advice
  • changing the subject or shifting focus from the client

Refer: support group, spiritual adviser if acceptable

cards.prompt: Caring for a dying client and the family
cards.promptHtml: Caring for a dying client and the family
cards.answerHtml:
Prevent abandonment:

  • answer call lights promptly, frequent contact
  • room near the nurses' station; at home, a central bed
  • let family stay

Psychosocial: support religious practices, prior coping, social services for finances and roles

Remember: hearing is the last sense lost: watch what is said near an unconscious client

Family: privacy, teach physical changes of active dying, offer care participation

cards.prompt: ADHD in children
cards.promptHtml: ADHD in children
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity

Dx: present before age 12 and in more than one setting; types: inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, combined

Risk: injury from impulsivity

Nursing:

  • calm, firm approach; get attention before directions
  • clear limits, consistency, physical activity
  • reward chart; focus on strengths

Meds: methylphenidate, dexmethylphenidate, amphetamine mixture, lisdexamfetamine; atomoxetine, guanfacine, clonidine

cards.prompt: Oppositional defiant disorder vs conduct disorder
cards.promptHtml: Oppositional defiant disorder vs conduct disorder
cards.answerHtml:
ODD:

  • negativity, defiance, argumentative, limit testing
  • shown at home toward the person best known
  • child does not see self as defiant; can progress to conduct disorder
  • meds not generally prescribed

Conduct:

  • violates others' rights and societal rules
  • lack of remorse, cruelty, property destruction, lying, truancy, weapons
  • childhood onset before age 10; adolescent onset after 10
  • watch for suicidal ideation

cards.prompt: DMDD vs intermittent explosive disorder
cards.promptHtml: DMDD vs intermittent explosive disorder
cards.answerHtml:
DMDD:

  • severe outbursts 3 or more times per week
  • in at least 2 settings
  • angry, irritable mood between outbursts
  • onset ages 6-18

IED:

  • episodic aggressive overreaction, then shame and regret
  • as early as age 6, typically 13-21; more males
  • can lead to hypertension and diabetes

IED meds: SSRIs, lithium, haloperidol, beta blockers, anticonvulsants

cards.prompt: Autism spectrum disorder
cards.promptHtml: Autism spectrum disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: poor eye contact, repetitive actions, strict routines; delayed language and cognition; more common in boys

Physical: sensory integration problems, sleep, digestive, feeding disorders, epilepsy

Nursing:

  • structured environment
  • short, concrete communication
  • plenty of notice before routine changes
  • redirect self-stimulating behavior with alternate play
  • physical, occupational, speech therapy referrals

Meds: SSRIs, risperidone, aripiprazole

cards.prompt: Depression in children and adolescents
cards.promptHtml: Depression in children and adolescents
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: irritability, temper tantrums, aggression, solitary play, sleep and appetite changes, poor school performance, substance use, hopelessness

Risk factors: family history, abuse, bullying (including cyberbullying), chronic illness

Nursing: depression and suicide assessment with immediate referral; ask about plan, means, weapons in the home

Remember: suicide is a leading cause of death ages 10-24

cards.prompt: PTSD and separation anxiety in children
cards.promptHtml: PTSD and separation anxiety in children
cards.answerHtml:
Separation anxiety: excessive distress when separated from parents; school phobia; depression common; can follow a stressor (death, move)

PTSD:

  • irritability, aggression, somatic complaints, sleep trouble
  • small children: repetitive play of the trauma

Nursing:

  • accept regression and defense mechanisms
  • meet needs during panic-level anxiety
  • group therapy; grief and trauma intervention (drawing, writing, play)

Meds: no FDA-approved antianxiety drug for children; SSRIs, duloxetine or clomipramine may be prescribed

cards.prompt: Disruptive child: what is the nurse's approach?
cards.promptHtml: Disruptive child: what is the nurse's approach?
cards.answerHtml:
Approach: calm, firm, respectful

Do:

  • model acceptable behavior
  • set clear limits and be consistent
  • give specific positive feedback
  • plan physical activity
  • help parents build a reward system
  • identify power-struggle issues

Behavior worsens: classroom (sustained attention) and unstructured play

Therapy: individual, group, family; CBT

cards.prompt: Prevention and safety teaching for adolescents
cards.promptHtml: Prevention and safety teaching for adolescents
cards.answerHtml:
Primary prevention: education, peer groups, mentoring

Safety:

  • gun and weapon control
  • seat belts
  • protective gear in high-impact sports

Sexual health: contraception and STI education; encourage abstinence but keep communication open

Refer: support groups, school nurse, counselor, police for bullying or safety concerns

History: ask about substance use, abuse, and self-injury

cards.prompt: Crisis: definition and duration
cards.promptHtml: Crisis: definition and duration
cards.answerHtml:
Crisis: acute, time-limited event (usually 4-6 weeks) where normal coping fails

Remember:

  • not pathological; client was previously well
  • personal: what is a crisis for one may not be for another
  • outcome is deterioration or growth

Features: sudden, seen as overwhelming, loss of communication with others, sense of displacement

Protective: support system, prior crisis experience

cards.prompt: Types of crisis: situational, maturational, adventitious
cards.promptHtml: Types of crisis: situational, maturational, adventitious
cards.answerHtml:
Situational (external): divorce, job loss, severe illness

Maturational (internal): new developmental stage, such as marriage or retirement

Adventitious: natural disasters, crimes such as rape, national disasters; not part of everyday life

cards.prompt: Four phases of a crisis
cards.promptHtml: Four phases of a crisis
cards.answerHtml:
1: rising anxiety from a threat; defenses increase

2: defenses fail; disorganized; trial-and-error

3: trial and error fails; severe/panic anxiety; flight or withdrawal

4: overwhelming anxiety, powerlessness, dissociation (depersonalization), depression, confusion, violence to self or others

cards.prompt: Crisis: what does the nurse do first?
cards.promptHtml: Crisis: what does the nurse do first?
cards.answerHtml:
Priority: safety first: screen for suicidal or homicidal ideation; admit if present

Then: meet physical needs

Then:

  • identify the current problem
  • take an active, directive role
  • set realistic, attainable goals
  • stay with the client, listen, make eye contact
  • short-term, focused action plan

Avoid: false reassurance and blaming ("Why did you let that happen?")

cards.prompt: Crisis: what does the nursing assessment include?
cards.promptHtml: Crisis: what does the nursing assessment include?
cards.answerHtml:
Ask about:

  • suicidal or homicidal ideation
  • client's perception of the event
  • support system
  • present coping skills
  • cultural or religious needs

Risk factors: unresolved losses, current stressors, comorbid illness, fatigue or pain, age and developmental stage

cards.prompt: Which drugs help a client in crisis, and which do not?
cards.promptHtml: Which drugs help a client in crisis, and which do not?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: benzodiazepines (alprazolam, diazepam, oxazepam; lorazepam also accepted) for anxiety; SSRIs and bupropion (paroxetine, fluoxetine) for depression

Use: adjuncts only, as prescribed

Not indicated for crisis alone:

  • lithium (bipolar)
  • risperidone, haloperidol (psychotic symptoms)

cards.prompt: Levels of crisis prevention: primary, secondary, tertiary
cards.promptHtml: Levels of crisis prevention: primary, secondary, tertiary
cards.answerHtml:
Primary: identify potential problems, teach coping, help with lifestyle changes

Secondary: interventions in an acute crisis that promote safety

Tertiary: support during recovery: outpatient clinics, rehabilitation, crisis stabilization, short-term residential

Staff: Critical Incident Stress Debriefing after exposure

cards.prompt: Crisis: client teaching and community resources
cards.promptHtml: Crisis: client teaching and community resources
cards.answerHtml:
Community: crisis stabilization, hotlines and warm lines, mobile and peer crisis services

Teach:

  • relaxation techniques
  • coping skills (assertiveness, parenting skills)
  • keep follow-up appointments

cards.prompt: Suicide myths: what is the truth?
cards.promptHtml: Suicide myths: what is the truth?
cards.answerHtml:
False (all):

  • people who talk about suicide never do it
  • asking about suicide plants the idea
  • they are only seeking attention
  • nothing can help someone who wants to die
  • ignoring or challenging threats reduces the behavior

Truth: clients are often ambivalent; asking directly will not give the idea; discuss it openly

cards.prompt: Suicide risk factors
cards.promptHtml: Suicide risk factors
cards.answerHtml:
Sex: females attempt more; adolescent, middle-aged, and older males die more

High-risk: veterans, LGBT, comorbid depression, substance use, schizophrenia, bipolar, personality disorders

Other:

  • family history, chronic or terminal illness
  • hopelessness, trauma or abuse
  • firearm access, unemployment
  • older adults: untreated depression, isolation, prior attempts

Highest rate: whites, then Native Americans (ATI order)

cards.prompt: Suicide warning signs and protective factors
cards.promptHtml: Suicide warning signs and protective factors
cards.answerHtml:
Warning:

  • overt comment ("no reason to go on living") or covert ("everything looks grim"): assess further
  • sudden calm or happiness after depression
  • old scars or lacerations

Protective: responsibility to children or partner, pregnancy, religious beliefs, life satisfaction, social support, coping skills, medical care

cards.prompt: Suicidal client: what is the priority assessment?
cards.promptHtml: Suicidal client: what is the priority assessment?
cards.answerHtml:
Priority: the plan: how lethal, how specific, and is the means available

Ask directly: "Are you thinking of suicide?"

If "no": follow up ("I can see you're very sad. Are you thinking about hurting yourself?")

Then: limit time alone, involve significant others, start suicide precautions, treat comorbid disorders

cards.prompt: Suicide precautions: what does the nurse do?
cards.promptHtml: Suicide precautions: what does the nurse do?
cards.answerHtml:
Supervision: constant one-on-one; document accountable staff with start and stop times; risk higher at staff rotation

Document: every 15 min

Environment:

  • search belongings with client present
  • remove sharps, belts, cords, glass
  • plastic utensils, counted
  • no private room; door open

Meds: make sure the client swallows them (hoarding); substitute less lethal drugs

Hands: always visible

cards.prompt: No-suicide contract and ECT
cards.promptHtml: No-suicide contract and ECT
cards.answerHtml:
Contract:

  • not legally binding
  • can build trust but never replaces other prevention
  • discouraged in crisis, intoxicated, psychotic, impulsive, or agitated clients

ECT: effective for suicidal ideation in depressive or psychotic disorders

Discharge: help client list support people, agencies, and phone numbers

cards.prompt: Levels of suicide intervention
cards.promptHtml: Levels of suicide intervention
cards.answerHtml:
Primary: community education and screening to find at-risk people

Secondary: individual in acute crisis: suicide precautions

Tertiary: support for survivors after a death by suicide; long-term therapy

Staff: a client's suicide can cause hopelessness, anger, denial: debrief and collaborate

Tool: SAFE-T monitors risk

cards.prompt: Medications for suicidal clients: key teaching
cards.promptHtml: Medications for suicidal clients: key teaching
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRIs (citalopram, fluoxetine, sertraline): lower overdose lethality; effect 1-3 weeks, maximum up to 2 months; monitor for worsening depression and intent; do not stop suddenly

Benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam): avoid alcohol; taper gradually over several weeks

Lithium: adequate sodium, fluids 2-3 L/day (Ch 23: at least 1.5-3 L), keep lab appointments

Second-generation antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, clozapine): preferred, fewer adverse effects

cards.prompt: Anger, aggression, and violence: definitions
cards.promptHtml: Anger, aggression, and violence: definitions
cards.answerHtml:
Anger: normal emotion; harmful when denied, suppressed, or expressed badly; may be secondary to depression, grief, anxiety, PTSD

Aggression: verbal or physical attack

Violence: goal-directed act intending to harm a specific person or object

Prodromal syndrome: early warning signs (pacing, grimacing, agitation)

Remember: clients with mental illness hurt themselves more than others

cards.prompt: Escalating anger: what does the nurse see?
cards.promptHtml: Escalating anger: what does the nurse see?
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like:

  • pacing, restlessness, hypersensitivity
  • intense or absent eye contact
  • clenched fists, waving arms, rapid breathing
  • leaning forward, tense
  • loud, rapid speech, shouting

Risk factors: past violence, poor impulse control, command hallucinations, intoxication, limit setting by the nurse

cards.prompt: De-escalating an aggressive client: steps
cards.promptHtml: De-escalating an aggressive client: steps
cards.answerHtml:
Steps:

  • respond quickly, stay calm
  • allow personal space; sit or stand at same level
  • nonthreatening, honest stance
  • offer choices; set limits calmly ("Walk with me to the day room")
  • encourage walking
  • medication if limits fail
  • 4-6 staff in sight (show of force)

Priority if violent: move others away first; ask staff to stay close

Avoid: "why" questions, demands, threats, walking away

cards.prompt: Seclusion and restraint: when and how?
cards.promptHtml: Seclusion and restraint: when and how?
cards.answerHtml:
Last resort under legal guidelines, only when there is risk of harm

Try first: verbal intervention, PRN medication, less stimulation, close observation, one-to-one

Risks: suffocation, strangulation; rarely death

Nursing: IM medication if needed; release as soon as the crisis is over and client is calm

After: debrief client and staff, document the entire incident

cards.prompt: Haloperidol (Haldol) for aggression
cards.promptHtml: Haloperidol (Haldol) for aggression
cards.answerHtml:
Class: first-generation antipsychotic, high potency (Ch 24)

Use: controls aggressive and impulsive behavior; used less than olanzapine or ziprasidone because of severe adverse effects

Monitor: EPS and parkinsonian effects, VS, hydration, muscle rigidity

Stop & report: muscle rigidity or fever (NMS risk, Ch 24)

Teach:

  • sips of water, fiber, stool softener if needed
  • limit sun, wear sunscreen and sunglasses
  • orthostatic hypotension, sedation

cards.prompt: Olanzapine (Zyprexa) and ziprasidone (Geodon)
cards.promptHtml: Olanzapine (Zyprexa) and ziprasidone (Geodon)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: atypical antipsychotics

Use: control aggressive and impulsive behavior; used more often than haloperidol (fewer severe adverse effects)

Teach: medication follow-up and support group after discharge

Also: SSRIs, lithium, and benzodiazepines can prevent violence by treating the underlying disorder

cards.prompt: Aggressive client: therapeutic vs nontherapeutic responses
cards.promptHtml: Aggressive client: therapeutic vs nontherapeutic responses
cards.answerHtml:
Therapeutic: "I need you to stop yelling and walk with me to the day room where we can talk." (calm limit plus activity)

Nontherapeutic:

  • "why" questions (imply criticism, cause defensiveness)
  • threats or closed statements ("You will not get your way by screaming")
  • probing before the client is ready
  • walking away or moving into the client's space

Aggressive communication: "You'd better listen to me"

cards.prompt: Cycle of violence
cards.promptHtml: Cycle of violence
cards.answerHtml:
1 Tension-building: minor anger, verbal abuse, minor violence; victim accepts blame

2 Acute battering: serious abuse; most violent and shortest

3 Honeymoon: perpetrator loving, sorry, promises to change; victim hopes

Then: cycle repeats with shorter intervals; repeated violence leads to powerlessness

cards.prompt: Types of family violence
cards.promptHtml: Types of family violence
cards.answerHtml:
Physical: pain or harm (shaken baby, striking, strangling)

Sexual: contact without consent

Emotional: humiliating, threatening, intimidating

Neglect: failure to provide physical or emotional care, education, or health care (including a stimulating environment)

Economic: failing to provide when funds are available (unpaid utilities)

cards.prompt: Child abuse: suspicious findings
cards.promptHtml: Child abuse: suspicious findings
cards.answerHtml:
Suspicious:

  • bruises on abdomen, back, buttocks (arms and legs expected)
  • injury does not match the explanation
  • bruises at different stages of healing; belt-buckle marks
  • glove or stocking burns; small round (cigarette) burns
  • spiral forearm fracture, multiple fractures
  • human bite marks

Risk: child under age 4, seen as different

cards.prompt: Shaken baby syndrome
cards.promptHtml: Shaken baby syndrome
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: intracranial hemorrhage, bulging fontanels, increased head circumference, retinal hemorrhage, respiratory distress, altered consciousness

Remember: any bruising before 6 months is suspicious; sunken fontanels are not expected here

Nursing: report suspected abuse; basic care of injuries; document

cards.prompt: Family violence: risk factors, victim, and perpetrator
cards.promptHtml: Family violence: risk factors, victim, and perpetrator
cards.answerHtml:
Greatest risk: when the victim tries to leave; pregnancy increases violence

Victim: low self-esteem, guilt and shame, protects the abuser and accepts blame, denial

Perpetrator: intimidation, strict disciplinarian, poor impulse control, substance use, likely abused as a child

Older adults: poor health, dependence on caregiver

Interview: private, direct, open-ended questions

cards.prompt: Family violence: priority nursing actions
cards.promptHtml: Family violence: priority nursing actions
cards.answerHtml:
Priority: help the client make a safety plan (safe places to live), even if the client declines to report

Report: all states require reporting suspected child or vulnerable adult abuse; civil and criminal penalties for failing

Also:

  • document subjective and objective data
  • treat injuries
  • refer, case management, shelter
  • tell the client when a protective services report is made

cards.prompt: Critical Incident Stress Debriefing
cards.promptHtml: Critical Incident Stress Debriefing
cards.answerHtml:
Level: tertiary crisis intervention in a safe place (staff after client violence, rescue workers after a disaster)

Steps:

  • purpose
  • facts
  • first thoughts
  • personal reactions
  • altered behaviors or physical changes
  • stress management teaching and anticipatory guidance
  • closure and referrals

Led by: RN facilitator

cards.prompt: Mass-casualty or community violence: early nursing interventions
cards.promptHtml: Mass-casualty or community violence: early nursing interventions
cards.answerHtml:
Early:

  • ensure physical and psychological safety
  • psychological first aid
  • reduce stress with panic-attack techniques
  • restore rest and sleep
  • connect to social supports and resources

Remember: natural disasters can cause mental health effects like human-made violence

Remember: a person with mental illness is no more likely to harm strangers than anyone else; best predictor of violence between strangers is a history of violence and crime

cards.prompt: A nurse is performing a mental status examination on a client who is newly admitted. The client states, "What would I do if there were a fire in my room? I would take the elevator down so I could leave quickly." Which of the following aspects of the mental status examination is the nurse evaluating, and what does this response indicate? A. Abstract thinking; the client's response is expected B. Judgment; the client's response shows impaired judgment C. Remote memory; the client's response shows intact memory D. Orientation; the client's response shows disorientation
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is performing a mental status examination on a client who is newly admitted. The client states, "What would I do if there were a fire in my room? I would take the elevator down so I could leave quickly." Which of the following aspects of the mental status examination is the nurse evaluating, and what does this response indicate?

  • A. Abstract thinking; the client's response is expected
  • B. Judgment; the client's response shows impaired judgment
  • C. Remote memory; the client's response shows intact memory
  • D. Orientation; the client's response shows disorientation
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Asking what the client would do in a hypothetical situation such as a fire assesses judgment. The client should give a logical, safe response. Taking an elevator during a fire is not a logical, safe response, so it shows impaired judgment. Abstract thinking is assessed by interpreting a cliché, remote memory by a verifiable past fact, and orientation by time, person, and place.

cards.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client who has depression and is being admitted to an acute mental health unit. Which of the following actions should the nurse take when conducting the interview? Select all that apply. A. Sit at the client's eye level B. Use a private, quiet space with adequate lighting C. Ask the client how they prefer to be addressed D. Summarize the interview and ask the client for feedback afterward E. Avoid questions about sleep, falls, and loss of energy to prevent distress
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is assessing a client who has depression and is being admitted to an acute mental health unit. Which of the following actions should the nurse take when conducting the interview? Select all that apply.

  • A. Sit at the client's eye level
  • B. Use a private, quiet space with adequate lighting
  • C. Ask the client how they prefer to be addressed
  • D. Summarize the interview and ask the client for feedback afterward
  • E. Avoid questions about sleep, falls, and loss of energy to prevent distress
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, C, D

Good interview technique includes a private, quiet, well-lit space (to accommodate vision and hearing deficits), asking the client's name preference, sitting or standing at the client's level, and summarizing afterward to get feedback. The nurse should specifically ask about difficulty sleeping, falls or other injuries, dizziness, incontinence, depression, and loss of energy, so option E is incorrect.

cards.prompt: A nurse is reviewing the plan of care for a client who has schizophrenia. Which of the following nursing actions should the nurse identify as milieu therapy? A. Administering the prescribed antipsychotic medication B. Teaching the client progressive muscle relaxation C. Modeling appropriate social behavior for the client D. Orienting the client to the unit rules and boundaries
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is reviewing the plan of care for a client who has schizophrenia. Which of the following nursing actions should the nurse identify as milieu therapy?

  • A. Administering the prescribed antipsychotic medication
  • B. Teaching the client progressive muscle relaxation
  • C. Modeling appropriate social behavior for the client
  • D. Orienting the client to the unit rules and boundaries
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Milieu therapy includes orienting the client to the physical setting, identifying rules and boundaries, ensuring a safe environment, and helping the client take part in appropriate activities. Giving medication is psychobiological. Teaching relaxation is health teaching or stress management. Modeling is a cognitive and behavioral therapy.

cards.prompt: A nurse in a school-based clinic is using the HEADSSS tool with an adolescent. Which of the following questions addresses the "S" for suicide/depression? A. "Do you feel safe walking home from school?" B. "Have you ever had any sexual encounters?" C. "Have you ever thought about hurting yourself or ending your life?" D. "Do you play on any sports teams?"
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse in a school-based clinic is using the HEADSSS tool with an adolescent. Which of the following questions addresses the "S" for suicide/depression?

  • A. "Do you feel safe walking home from school?"
  • B. "Have you ever had any sexual encounters?"
  • C. "Have you ever thought about hurting yourself or ending your life?"
  • D. "Do you play on any sports teams?"
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

In HEADSSS, the suicide/depression domain asks whether the client is at risk for suicide or self-injury or shows signs of depression. Safety addresses abuse in the home and neighborhood violence. Sexuality addresses sexual activity. Activities addresses sports and peer interaction. Asking directly about self-harm is appropriate and does not increase risk (general knowledge).

cards.prompt: A nurse on an inpatient unit observes a client who is agitated and pacing. The client has begun yelling at a peer. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first? A. Request a prescription for mechanical restraints B. Verbally encourage the client to calm down C. Place the client in a monitored seclusion room D. Administer a chemical restraint without a prescription
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse on an inpatient unit observes a client who is agitated and pacing. The client has begun yelling at a peer. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?

  • A. Request a prescription for mechanical restraints
  • B. Verbally encourage the client to calm down
  • C. Place the client in a monitored seclusion room
  • D. Administer a chemical restraint without a prescription
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Verbal interventions are the least restrictive method and are attempted first when a client is becoming aggressive. Diversion, a quiet low-stimulation environment, and a PRN medication come next, then seclusion, then restraints only when all less restrictive measures fail. Restraint or seclusion should be used for the shortest duration necessary and never for staff convenience or punishment.

cards.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who is in seclusion. Which of the following actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply. A. Offer food and fluids B. Monitor vital signs C. Offer toileting D. Leave the client alone until the next provider visit E. Document the client's behavior and the time of release from seclusion
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is caring for a client who is in seclusion. Which of the following actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

  • A. Offer food and fluids
  • B. Monitor vital signs
  • C. Offer toileting
  • D. Leave the client alone until the next provider visit
  • E. Document the client's behavior and the time of release from seclusion
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, C, E

Per facility protocol the nurse monitors safety, behavior, and physical needs, which includes offering food and fluids, toileting, vital signs, and pain assessment. The nurse documents objective behavior, interventions, medications, and the time the client was released. The client must be monitored regularly (documentation every 15 to 30 min or per policy), so leaving the client alone until the provider arrives is unsafe.

cards.prompt: A client who has a psychotic disorder saw two staff members talking and asks the nurse whether they were discussing the client. They were, but the nurse answers, "No, that was about something else." Which of the following ethical principles has the nurse violated? A. Autonomy B. Justice C. Veracity D. Beneficence
cards.promptHtml:
A client who has a psychotic disorder saw two staff members talking and asks the nurse whether they were discussing the client. They were, but the nurse answers, "No, that was about something else." Which of the following ethical principles has the nurse violated?

  • A. Autonomy
  • B. Justice
  • C. Veracity
  • D. Beneficence
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Veracity is honesty in dealing with a client. Denying a conversation that did happen is a lie; the nurse should give a truthful, brief answer about what the team discussed. Autonomy is the right to make one's own decisions, justice is fair and equal treatment, and beneficence is doing good.

cards.prompt: A client is voluntarily admitted to a mental health facility and states, "I do not want to take the medication that the provider prescribed." Which of the following responses by the nurse is appropriate? A. "You signed a form agreeing to all treatments, so you have to take it." B. "I will tell the provider you are refusing, and we can discuss your concerns." C. "I will mix it into your juice so you will not taste it." D. "You can be committed involuntarily if you refuse."
cards.promptHtml:
A client is voluntarily admitted to a mental health facility and states, "I do not want to take the medication that the provider prescribed." Which of the following responses by the nurse is appropriate?

  • A. "You signed a form agreeing to all treatments, so you have to take it."
  • B. "I will tell the provider you are refusing, and we can discuss your concerns."
  • C. "I will mix it into your juice so you will not taste it."
  • D. "You can be committed involuntarily if you refuse."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

A client admitted voluntarily is considered competent and has the right to refuse medication and treatment. The nurse respects autonomy, explores the client's concerns, and notifies the provider. Hiding medication in food would be deceptive (violating veracity) and a battery risk. Threatening commitment as coercion is inappropriate.

cards.prompt: A client who has major depressive disorder says, "I feel like nothing will ever get better." The nurse responds, "You feel that nothing will get better?" Which of the following therapeutic communication techniques is the nurse using? A. Restating B. Presenting reality C. Focusing D. Giving information
cards.promptHtml:
A client who has major depressive disorder says, "I feel like nothing will ever get better." The nurse responds, "You feel that nothing will get better?" Which of the following therapeutic communication techniques is the nurse using?

  • A. Restating
  • B. Presenting reality
  • C. Focusing
  • D. Giving information
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Restating repeats the client's own words (or main idea) back to the client to confirm the message and encourage the client to continue. Presenting reality dispels delusions or faulty beliefs, focusing helps the client concentrate on one important point, and giving information provides facts the client needs for decisions. The nurse should also allow extra time for clients who have major depressive disorder to respond.

cards.prompt: A nurse is caring for an older adult client who has hearing loss and is grieving the death of a spouse. Which of the following actions should the nurse take to promote communication? Select all that apply. A. Face the client when speaking B. Minimize noise and other distractions C. Allow plenty of time for the client to respond D. Ask the client "Why do you feel so sad?" E. Consider whether the client needs amplification
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is caring for an older adult client who has hearing loss and is grieving the death of a spouse. Which of the following actions should the nurse take to promote communication? Select all that apply.

  • A. Face the client when speaking
  • B. Minimize noise and other distractions
  • C. Allow plenty of time for the client to respond
  • D. Ask the client "Why do you feel so sad?"
  • E. Consider whether the client needs amplification
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, C, E

Adapted techniques for older adults include facing the client, minimizing distractions, allowing plenty of time to respond, recognizing that amplification might be needed, and asking caregivers or family about deficits. "Why" questions are a barrier to therapeutic communication (ATI ch 3, p.25); they can make the client feel defensive and pressured to justify feelings (general knowledge).

cards.prompt: A client who is anxious about an upcoming discharge says, "I don't think I can handle going home." Which of the following nurse responses is an example of a barrier to therapeutic communication? A. "Tell me more about what worries you." B. "It sounds like you are afraid of being alone." C. "You are going to do great. Don't worry." D. "What would it be like if you did not have anxiety?"
cards.promptHtml:
A client who is anxious about an upcoming discharge says, "I don't think I can handle going home." Which of the following nurse responses is an example of a barrier to therapeutic communication?

  • A. "Tell me more about what worries you."
  • B. "It sounds like you are afraid of being alone."
  • C. "You are going to do great. Don't worry."
  • D. "What would it be like if you did not have anxiety?"
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Telling the client not to worry and that all will go well is false reassurance, and it minimizes the client's feelings.
